I had my eye on this game since it showed up on Steam, eagerly waiting for it's release. I wasn't sold on the 40€ price tag however, so I waited.
Fast forward to Winter Sale 2019, the game is 60% off, but the reviews are worrying. Many of them list negatives (more on those later) and of course some people love it.
I don't think anyone can accurately tell if they're going to like a ~30 hour game, based on the 2 hours that you can spend on any game before refunding. So I tried the game through 'alternative methods', decided I like it, and bought it on Steam.

If you're reading this, you probably came across the "most voted for" reviews that list negatives (and/or positives), and I have to say, some of them are straight up not true (negatives such as: "Enemies do not play by the same rules as you"). And you definitely don't "need to go to the wiki", to beat the game. Nor is it unfair, that enemies surround you and stab you to death.. since when is that a negative in games? But I digress.

Outward is an epic adventure in a fantasy world, where you play as a SIMPLE man.
The world is not your friend.. personal needs (food, water, sleep), disease, weather, wild animals, bandits are all out there to make your life harder. Of course you can prepare for all of the above, but sometimes the unexpected happens and you have to think fast..

When you die, the game throws a dice, and decides what happens to you (depending on the situation you died in).
60% of the time, it isn't a big setback (or I'm just hella lucky), 35% of the time it's a little annoying and 5% of the time you might feel like all is lost, and rather start again.
100% of the time, however, you can get your shit together and stand up again.

It's true, the game does not hold your hand much, and if you open the map you'll only see the major landmarks marked on it, so you'll have to navigate the world by looking around and using the compass.

The game itself has 4 main regions and believe me when I say, the map makes them look WAY BIGGER than they actually are, from one landmark, you can see many others, so I really don't understand other people complaining about the death penalty being "throw you in random location, good luck". It's pretty easy to navigate.

Talking about regions.. the soundtrack is absolutely awesome in 99% of the game. The voice acting.. not so much. Not sure why they decided to add voice acting, as there's only a few generic lines most of the time and not the exact info you need, so you'll have to read a bit.

The combat system is fine, in fact I love the backpack mechanic!
The magic is a little underwhelming however, you have to "unlock" mana which lets you use spells (which is totally fine, the SPELLS ARE THE UNDERWHELMING PART), even then however you'll run out of mana pretty quick.
You can't really play a full on mage from the start, you need very specific gear, weapons and learned skills from trainers, unless you're fine eating mana restoring food and chugging potions.

SIDE NOTE:
This game is NOT dark souls. If I had to compare it to anything, I'd compare it to Two Worlds (2, epic game btw, best magic system, wish more games used it). Sure there are bosses, sure enemies hit hard, yes you can roll, you can even LOCK ON, WOW, truly a dark souls game.
It is not.

Your health and stamina (the MAXIMUM amount) will decrease (slowly) if they are not "topped off". Meaning, when you sprint all day long, your maximum stamina will decrease over time. All this is reverted by sleeping, or using consumables.
I have to say though, this mechanic has never affected me in any way.

FOOD! It rots in your bag, it rots in your stash, it ROTS overtime. It's a mechanic that can be 100% ignored, just like the maximum health/stamina decrease in my opinion.

The game doesn't have fast travel, and I highly agree with this decision as it would ruin some quests/events that you might unknowingly run into. Running does get tedious after a while though (you'll have to decide for yourself if it's too much or not), and sadly, there's nothing that will change it outside of certain armors with bonus movespeed.

While you're running around, you'll probably feel the game is a little empty in places, some worse, some better. Not that bad honestly.

The story is alright, there are 3 "factions" you can join, and the events happen in parallel, so I highly encourage you to play all 3 sides of the story. You can only join one "faction" per character.

There's a legacy system in the game, albeit totally useless.
Throughout the game there are 4 chests in which you can put ONE item. When you make a new character, you can choose a legacy character, which makes those chests contain the items that were put in them.
Except by the time you get to these chests, you're at the end game anyway.
So you're better off just using split-screen to give items to new characters.
Why couldn't they include passing down skills or other stats? Hella useless.

AI could be better in places, but overall it's OK. Maybe it's better that they are easy to cheese sometimes, otherwise if you're just starting out, it seems impossible to beat.

There are a lot of invisible walls, some of which I don't even understand, instead of a steep mountain, they put an invisible wall on the edge of the desert area, like what?
There's also no JUMPing. ):

Overall, I think the devs did alright and made an epic adventure game with lots to explore, and the fact that you can play all of it in co-op, is awesome.

The major thing I don't agree with, is it's price.
I can not justify 40€ for it, and everyone who can is delusional.. FACT. I would say fair enough to about 20-25€ TOPS.

A lot could be improved on, legacy, AI, camera/mouse smoothing etc.. I feel like if just a few more of these systems were executed worse, the thumb would point down.

There are a lot of bugs also, but most of them aren't gamebreaking, happen very rarely, or happen in the menu.

And who the fuck cares how many people worked on it? That is simply not a factor when determining how good or bad a game is.

[h1] MULTIPLAYER [/h1]

The game came out with 2 player local/online coop (there are mods that remove this limitation for the cost of stability), enemies do scale with the number of players, although the game becomes considerably easier due to the limitless cheesing of enemies (in my opinion).

Only the host character (aka savefile) progresses IN THE STORY, meaning that players (be it host or not) will KEEP their items/skills/what have you, when they leave the coop session.
Quest rewards however will only go to the host player (which isn't a big deal, quest rewards aren't OP, nor mandatory).

I have to say though, if you think "why buy a coop game if I have to play the same story twice, so my friend can progress as well".
I'll let you in on a little secret: there are 3 main story paths you can take. All of them worth playing.

So if you've finished one of them, well.. enjoy the second one (on their savefile), being that much easier with your well equipped characters!

[h1]DO NOT BE AFRAID OF THIS GAME![/h1]

I know... if you are reading this you are probably thinking about buying this game, you are an avid RPG player. 

Outward looks so appealing to you but you are not sure if it will fulfill all you want in an Open World RPG Survival game and most of all, you are scared of the "Souls-like" tag right there! You love roleplaying, you love survival, you love immersion, you love huge diversity of items, places, enemies and also a good and FAIR challenge... 

I started playing Outward very recently (some people could state that I don't know the game very well) however I will still try my best to convince you that: yes, this game might be for you! 

[h1]1) About the Difficulty:[/h1] 

Ok, the game is difficult alright! But I wouldn't say that this is a "Souls-like" difficulty! The beginning is really harsh, you will be overwhelmed by most enemies outside the gates but seriously, if you have played other "old school" RPGs like Risen and Gothic, you will probably know that you never start a game killing demons and dragons... everything demands a preparation and planning, Outward is on that category. 

Even Skyrim, for example, if you play in Legendary Difficulty and go outside with a weak armor, you will be killed by a mere Giant Mudcrab! You will realize that "Ok, I need to prepare. I need better gear, maybe some skills/perks and potions". 

Dying in Outward doesn't mean you lose the game (unless you play in Hardcore), you will wake up in a different location and the outcomes of your death depends on the circumstances of your defeat. If you are killed by Hyenas you will wake up in their Nest, if you die by bandits you wake up on their Camp and so on... that much I already learned! Hyenas won't steal your gear but bandits might do so! You can recover all your lost items usually in the place where you wake up. 

If you can't find your backpack next to you, just look around and you might find your items on a chest... you can consult the Outward wiki, this mechanic is very complex but at least, I hope you understood that the game is not really difficult, its not unfair, it just demands that you prepare for things! 

I find games like Conan Exiles way harder than Outward and that "Souls-like" tag is misplaced, in my honest opinion. 

[h1]2) About the Survival:[/h1] 

Being brief... its a standard survival mechanic. Hunger, Thirst and Sleep, they do affect your stats with buffs and debuffs depending on your conditions but its nothing really complex. There are diseases in this game, so far I didn't got any trouble with that but I already noticed that there are concoctions that heal you and apparently some diseases can be cured by sleeping and keeping yourself well-nourished. 

[h1]3) About the Roleplaying:[/h1] 

There is a Character Creation and Customization Interface but nothing too much detailed.

You are pretty much free to do whatever you want. Some places are restricted to be accessed only after quests but overall, you can go anywhere you want. So far, I've been farming Silver to build my strenght the best I can! Right now I am roleplaying as a fisherman, because I've realized that some fish can be sold by a good price and I am slowly getting a good gear to become an adventurer and later on, maybe join a Faction which I am not sure right now... maybe the Holy Faction!

The game constantly reminds you that you are not a hero, rather, you are just a commoner supposed to find your place in a harsh world and at the very beginning you will learn that. When you go out of your house, there will be a mob demanding you to pay lots of money in compensation of the bad deeds made by your grandmother, in the world of Outward, the descendants must pay for the mistakes of their ancestors and that is just the beginning of a whole world of unforgiveness! 

[h1]4) Hints:[/h1] 

Well, so far I can tell you that Fishing is a good and safe option to farm Silver, your only expense is a Harpoon. 

My gameplay improved a lot after I bought a Flintlock from the merchant at the gates. I suppose you could use a bow to kill enemies from high-ground but at least for me, it was not a good strategy... 

Bandages and Rags helps a lot! 

Invest in Weapons with high Impact value, they are better to stagger enemies and helps you to hit more times!

So far, this is all I can say...

[h1]5) How this game could improve:[/h1] 

What I am mostly missing here is a Workshop. Outward does have a Modding Community and you can find some pretty interesting mods in Nexus, however, I would still enjoy more if we could have a Steam Workshop for Outward! 

It could help engage more people in the Modding scene. 

So far, this is all I have to say about Outward (I'll update this Review if needed). 

Again, do not be afraid to play this game! Its not as difficult as it portrays itself and its not unfair as some negative reviews says! Just be open-minded and have patience!!

I avoided Outward based on most of the negative reviews regarding mechanics and melee combat. Given that my ankle is currently broken and I've been losing my mind, I decided to take the plunge anyway to purchase the game. At worst, I figured, I'd refund it within 2 hours if things really were as bad as people said they were. I mean hell, the game looks gorgeous (and it is). 

They were wrong.

I see/feel nothing wrong with melee combat.  It's all about timing, and I have yet to die to any enemy thus far. I've even already managed to completely wipe 2 dungeons, wait for them to respawn, then clear them again. Archery takes some time to get used to, but it's definitely passable. I don't know about magic usage since I don't tend to play mage-type characters. Either way, with limited passive/active skills, melee combat is nowhere near as bad as people are making it out to be. Blocking works perfectly fine, it plays like a slower version of Dark Souls, which really is the best comparison that can be made here. Sure, enemies can chain together moves a lot quicker than you can, but time them out. People who I see criticizing this are no doubt trying to rush the combat along and paying the price for their impatience. You must be patient with the combat in this game.

The survival mechanics are pretty much able to be ignored for the most part. You rarely get thirsty or hungry unless sleeping for hours on end; being hot, cold, or wet is only a worry if you have to sleep outside; stamina is a bit of a concern if you're always sprinting everywhere (your max stamina goes down semi-noticeably) and it's depletion rate is otherwise determined by your armor. Eating gives buffs, drinking gives buffs (even stam regen!), and sleeping gives buffs. 

As far as people calling it a walking simulator, they obviously aren't going very far or they're avoiding encounters. Anytime I go out, I fight roughly 8-14 bandits or monsters, even toppling a few bandit lieutenants or heavily armored bandits. Going from place-to-place is never a bore, albeit perhaps tedious once you fight enough. Oh, and dungeons are pretty dope too. 

Either way, I've managed to rake up 6k silver within hours just by grinding 2 dungeons and fighting enemies outside of town. I have yet to even take any of the two sides for the main quest in the starting town. So.. yeah. People are over-exaggerating their grievances with the game. Nothing anyone has said negatively about the game is actually THAT bad. At this point, the only thing I would change is how easy it is to grind for silver, and maybe at a keyboard binding for actual walking. Oh, and for this kind of game, I would more than appreciate a first-person view camera. For what this game is and offers, I consider it an oversight for the lack of that specific featurette.

Anyway, I recommend the game. I would still get it on sale if you can, but if you're on the fence and determined to buy it one way or the other, take the plunge. You'll get more of a feel for the game before your two hour refund window is up.

I've now played through each of the game's main questlines, across three different characters, and I think that this is the best 7/10 game I've ever played. When I first started playing I really wasn't sure about it and even considered a refund but as I kept coming back it slowly grew on me. It's janky, made on a budget, and there are plenty of questionable design choices, but overall I think it offers something pretty unique even apart from it's obvious influences like Gothic. This isn't an RPG that you're playing for the quests and dialogue or even the loot and character building (although I think those last two are actually pretty good). It's truly focused on exploration at your own pace and those other elements are just there to tease out your curiosity, add some form of progression and to nudge you towards interesting places.

The way in which the gameplay systems connect to each other can actually be pretty elegant which surprised me. When you think eurojank you don't expect great balance but generally the economy and class system holds up. It's an RPG with no levels or exp so all progression is based on equipment and skills, which you purchase. This creates an interesting dynamic where cash is king but getting the cash requires an investment in time and resources like. You won't be making bank just killing bandits out in the field, you need to go deep into scary places to get the good shit. That's where the backpack system really shines imo. It's neat that your inventory is actually a physical item that you carry around (and can drop on the ground to give you a better combat roll) and the way carry weight works is similarly smart. When you become overburdened you're not immediately stuck, you just lose some movement speed which decreases further as you become more full of stuff. This gradiant kind of let's you decide for yourself just how far you're willing to go, keeping in mind that with no form of fast travel you'll be lugging everything back manually. This is pretty much the main gameplay loop, deciding how far you can travel while still being able to comfortably make it back to town while maximizing your loot gains, and it's pretty engrossing to me. The survival game elements actually work well here too, and aren't really obtrusive at all. This is because you're very rarely eating/drinking/sleeping just because you have to fill a meter but because you're actively seeking the bonuses that food or sleep confer.

Of course you'll be fighting things while you're off exploring and I for one think the combat system is perfectly functional. It's kind of simple but with just enough moment to moment decision making to keep it interesting. The previously mentioned backpack drop manuver is a good example of one of the nice little touches that add a lot. So dropping your backpack gives you a better roll, which is great, but it also has some disadvantages. For one, you're often fighting in caves or tombs or whatever and your lantern is usually tied to your backpack. Shit gets dark in Outward so if the fight takes you out of the area of your downed light source you can get truly fucked. For two, your backpack has all your shit in it, so if say you want to chug a potion or douse yourself with water to keep you from burning to death you'll have to either grab it mid fight or do without. The way death works is quite unique. You never actually die in Outward, instead you're knocked unconscious and then some event happens depending on where you died or what killed you. Some friendly mercenaries might drag you back to town, or you might get thrown in a prison and have to escape or just end up back at the beginning of the dungeon (or sometimes even deeper in). These are pretty hit or miss for me. Some seem overly generous, like just sticking you back at the start. Others can be a nightmare, like stranding you deep in the dungeon sometimes separated from your backpack. Overall, if there is one thing I really like about the combat it's that generally encounters feel significant. Often there will only be 1 to 3 tough fights between you and the end of the dungeon and that really incentivizes you actually use everything at your disposal (potions, food, buffs, skill cooldowns, etc.).

I mentioned that I've played with three different characters, each with a different build (roughly corresponding to a mage/fighter/rogue) and I was really pleased by not just how different each felt to play but also by how similarly powerful they all ended up. Each had their own strengths and weaknesses but none of them felt vastly over or under powered. I've seen some things about this being a classless system and that's a bit off. There are classes, but only some of their skills are exclusive, most are available for anyone to learn. Also you get to pick three class specializations so the exact build you make can be pretty flexible. If I have any general advice for character building it would be that you can get quite far without specializing so wait awhile before you decide even if you have a build in mind. Also don't do what I did on my first character and take a bunch of mana before you actually have access to good spells lol.

There are three main questlines, each centered around one of the three major factions and this aspect more than any other really harkens back to Gothic. The story is focused mostly on tribal politics with a bit of mystical lore and it's really not bad. Totally adequate story for this sort of game, excluding the voice acting which I found distractingly bad and turned it off. Most importantly though is that the quests do a good job of pointing you towards new areas and rarely feel urgent enough that you feel bad taking some time off to do your own thing. Notably, even having done all the major quests there were still dungeons that they never took me too. If you're a normal person and only do one questline there will be tons of places left unseen. One of the factions doesn't even require you to visit one of the four regions at all. These quests are really just supplemental material, and that's underscored by the ending which is essentially “great work, now go fuck around”.

To camp out on the four regions for a minute: they're spectacular imo. Again, this game was made on a budget so everything looks a bit last gen and yet they've done a great job with what they had to work with. Each region has its own theme and personality with a unique set of challenges to consider. I just loved romping around in these places and poking into dungeons I shouldn't have been in. Also got to give a shoutout to the wonderful overworld tracks, especially the hallowed marsh theme.

The game doesn't feel nearly as full, and alive as some people make it seem. The towns are very bland with mute npcs, nothing is really furnished, you can't interact with anything other than shinies, chests and junk piles and over all feels like a half-finished project. Combat is sloooow, very clunky and can be frustrating. Using magic is similar and will make you want to just use a bow or a gun instead of having to set up combos for spells for little damage/reward. The graphics (For players and Humanoids/NPCS) seem very EQ2-esque and feel like they need a once over as well. One thing positive I will say is that many of the enemies and surrounding areas are very well designed and beautiful. Overall, this feels like more of a $9.99 (edit) to $15.00 type game and should be put on "In-Development" status until more life gets infused into it.

*edit* Don't get me wrong, I WANT to love this game, and I am still on the fence. I know that a small team developed this game, and I applaud them for making it. Heck, it would take me years to even come close to what they have made. It still feels unpolished though and has areas in which it could improve, many are pointed out in the reviews. How to fix it? I do not know. Perhaps modding tools, or taking on more people for an update? Allowing community contributions for writing, story lines and/or voice acting might give this game a significant boost as well. Feel free to add to this.

I think I have enough game time to finally review this game.

Good:
- The maps are absolutely fantastic! It eases the pain of running long distances without anything resembling fast travel, when you can just enjoy the eye candy of the landscapes as you travel.
- I think the game's combat and exploration is perfectly fair. You get beaten to a bloody pulp if you don't focus and prepare properly.
- Death is a possibility. You never now where you'll end up when you pass out. Though imo it needs more variety after you've played for some time.
- After you're familiar with the skills in game, making a full build that suits your current play style is extremely satisfying.
- Crafting is simple enough and after you learn how the logic of the recipes work, it's actually pretty easy to find correct combinations on your own, without having to buy the recipes.
- The way the quests work. The game let's you fail your quests/quest steps, and some quests have nearly the same outcome no matter what happens, but some quests you can REALLY FAIL, and it has serious consequences that leave you amazed to what the heck just happened.

Bad and OK
- If you ask me the character textures are horrible... You make a character that you think looks OK, but it's still worse than destroying your character's look in Elder Scrolls Oblivion.
- Back to combat: The combat is kind of stiff and clunky. It's an ok combat system, but I bet it could be much more fluid. This "bad" thing is ok, because even if it's not entirely satisfactory, I still feel it fits considering the feeling of the game.
- Breakthrough skills are way too expensive for the first character. It'd be nice if, say the first breakthrough skills would be discounted for a character or something.
- Story: Not necessarily bad, but there other indie games out there that have waaay better stories to tell. But in the good section I mentioned how the quests work, and that makes up some of the lacking story.

Overall:
When I first saw this games trailer, I bought it the next day without hesitation. Never regretted a single moment in the game. It get's tedious and boring at some point, but if you just push through the boredom, you'll notice that you sort of can't play anything else at the moment.
I'm not sure if I'd pay the full 39,99€ at this point (most likely would), and I'm yet to judge if the DLC was worth the 20€.
But still after the 130hrs I have played, I can easily say that it's among the best games I've ever played. This is mainly because of the time we live in and the current game industry, when games constantly disappoint you with some crap.
Outward hasn't disappointed me a single time during my gameplay, and what I find it lacking is because I've played it for so long that I'd like to see some spicing up here and there.

Personally, I think many people buy this game thinking it's going to be a "souls-like" but that's not the case.

This is an all out survival game, your character gets thirsty, hungry, hot, cold etc. You will have to change equipment or drink certain potions to accommodate to all of these conditions. You get fatigued, have to sleep to restore all of your stats but even this has negative effects such as burning your mana recovery.

When starting out you will have a blood debt of 150 silver, and only have so many days to pay it off. To be able to do this I recommend the following:

- The best way is to grab a bandage or life potion, go through Cierzo storage which can be found at the end of the docks, run through the cave (Troglodyte enemies are here so be careful) eventually there will be a drop down and a door/opening through to the beach. Whilst on the beach search the nearby rocks to find Michel, hand him a bandage or life potion and you will receive a Writ of Tribal Favor which can be handed in to pay off the debt.

- Alternatively, grab a pickaxe, go to the centre of the map and mine mana stone veins. This has a chance of mining Hackmanite which sells for roughly 50 silvers each.

Moving on, I see many comments about the combat, and how many struggle to down enemies straight out of the gates of Cierzo (first town). Every enemy has a break bar as such, it is the grey bar underneath the health bar. You will not do nearly as much damage until this break bar is depleted and they stun, so keep that in mind when playing this game.

I suggest buying an iron halberd with the silver you have at the beginning of the game and go to the guard that is blocking your way out off the gates of Cierzo. Once you have a waterskin, tell him that you want to venture out whilst holding the halberd and he will teach you a skill called "Moon Swipe". This skill paired with "Push Kick" is an incredible combo for starting out. I suggest using push kick into the moon swipe. 

Kill a few Hyena's that are walking about (cave found on the path to the right as soon as you leave Cierzo) and try to retrieve 2 x predator bones. After this, go into the crafting menu with the Iron halberd, 2 x Predator bones & a piece of linen cloth to get a Fang Halberd. This halberd will help you down enemies quicker as it inflicts 45% build up of bleed damage.

Banger, probably in my top 10 games OAT but requires time to learn and understand. 

I see a lot of negative reviews comparing this game to Dark Souls or Elden Ring. Let me tell you if you think that you are going to be disappointed, this game IS NOT Dark Souls nor Elden Ring but something else. If you want an experience like those games go play something else.

The combat is actually not so bad when you learn it people struggle with it because they leave Cierzo and immediately try to fight hyenas and bandits without understanding the basics, and the magic system is unique and fun to use. But again, both of these things will require time and patience so you can properly understand them. There are also survival elements in the game, but they are really simple. There's a lot of food and water, and sleeping is not a big problem.

Another great critique is the walking everywhere, since there's no fast travel and the maps can be fairly big. This problem persists throughout the full game, so keep in mind that you can spend 30 minutes or so just traveling from a city to another. If that's a dealbreaker, maybe pass this game. Outward is a strange game. You can think of it like an open-world souls-like with survival elements, but the game is not kind to folks who may already be familiar with souls-like combat or survival games. The world is populated with enemies but, in most circumstances, there isn't a clear benefit to fighting them. You'll stumble across dozens of ingredients without a good way to identify what they're for or how they'll help you. You'll walk into an area and start dying very rapidly from weather or status conditions that you've haven't had a chance to learn about yet. When you die, you're likely to end up in a bizarre situation that you didn't get to prepare for. Like all games, Outward needs you to learn how to play within its ruleset, but it doesn't do a great job teaching those mechanics to you.

Yet, I still recommend the game. If you get past those early hurdles (and if you don't that's okay, too; there are lots of other great games) then you'll be free to experience the charm this game has to offer. That charm comes from the environments, the dungeons, in planning ahead for your next journey and possible fights along the way, in constructing a character build, and even in the lethality of combat and the death scenarios.

Exploration is king in Outward and there's a lot of cool stuff to see and find. Exploration, more than any other game element finances your character growth. If you need that exploration and growth to be in service of a clearly set end goal, you may not find this game as fulfilling as others. It can offer a few concrete goals, such as the main story or tough boss fights, but they feel a bit separate from the core gameplay loop. As an example of this separation, you can choose when to continue the main quest after a clearly punctuated intermission. To compare it to another game, it's like choosing when to do Bleak Falls Barrow in Skyrim (just a similar example; playing Outward is not like playing Skyrim). In Skyrim, a significant element of character growth is tied to completing that quest. But in Outward, there's no such gatekeeping. There's perks to completing certain quests and doing them well, or in siding with certain factions, but you can finish most of your build and go nearly anywhere without progressing the story at all. In fact, at the time of this review, I haven't actually done much of the main quest. ^_^;

If you're not sure whether this game is for you, here's what I'd recommend if you're willing to give it a quick try before a possible refund: play the opening sequence, get to the point when you can leave the first town and then go explore for a bit (all easy to do within 2 hours). Don't worry too much about the quest you've been given; it can be a bit stressful and it's not very representative of the rest of the game. You can try the tutorial first, but I'd recommend to do that after exploring (it's always available), since it can take a bit of time with all the info it shares. Here's some tips that may help you.

Outward is a survival game in the sense that everything you do costs something: resources and weapon durability are common to other games, but you'll also spend other things like max health and stamina, especially in fights. If you sleep to recover those, then you'll lose max mana. It can be frustrating early on when the first enemies out the door are wailing on you and you're only getting weaker as they hit you. But, enemies don't necessarily have anything useful for you to loot, and since there's no character experience, it's often better not to engage. You will eventually have to fight, so when you feel up for it, shadowbox with your weapon to get a feel for its timing and range, then practice on enemies outdoors, or better yet, [spoiler]lure enemies into each other so that you can see how they behave[/spoiler]. If you don't like your weapon, there's one of every type lying around in the first town. The most difficult thing to adapt from other games is that enemies don't stagger when you hit them, at least not at first, and the AI will see your attack as an opening to counterattack. If all else fails, just run away and recover. When you die, because dying is a near essential part of the game, you'll probably end up somewhere you don't recognize, weakened, with debuffs and [spoiler]maybe enemies nearby and ready to attack[/spoiler]. Mercifully, the only things you may lose upon death are time (in the in-game calendar) and possibly a bit of money. [spoiler]Losing time only matters if your doing a timed quest[/spoiler]. You may not have your stuff on or next to you after death, but look around and you'll find it soon. Defeat scenarios are meant to be a bit stressful, but accept that you can always recover from them and that mindset can help pull you through an otherwise dastardly challenge.

While it has lots of positive elements, and a very enticing premise, this game suffers from some truly awful design. 

The idea of an open world adventure where you don't magically "level up" at a certain point... where you're not a walking god for whom the entire universe was built....where you don't feel like you're walking past exhibitions in a museum but instead a small and vulnerable traveler in a big world. That's a cool idea! 

I wish I could say the game delivers the concept well, but the systems are so poorly designed that it punishes the player at nearly every turn. Outward also commits several cardinal sins for an open world. Firstly, without ever explaining why, EVERY SINGLE THING you meet in the wild (creature, animal, human, etc) will attack you instantly. There's no emergent dialogue or anything to promote immersion. You have this black and white world where town is impossibly "safe" from EVERYTHING and outside the gates the universe will do everything it can to kill you.

Oh and it will succeed. Between weather/seasons, disease, statuses from enemies and sometimes just dumb luck on judging the height of something or the difficulty of an enemy... you die a lot. If you've played games like Dark Souls and such, that's no big deal. One thing that gets truly tiresome, however, is being spawned at one of the same random locations each time you do and then slogging your way back to where you were to die again. 

The economy is absurd, largely unexplained and totally broken. Everything seems so expensive, but a quick click of the youtube will make you rich in short order... so long as you can stomach the grind of "buy mats. sleep three days. make pots. sell pots. buy mats. sleep three days." essentially forever. 

Split screen coop was one of the driving things that go me to try this game, but even as a team its just too flipping hard... not good hard either. It's janky, weird off-kilter combat doesn't seem to ever make it intuitive when to block, or what weapon/strategy is a good choice. You bump into hugely over-powered enemies when you have essentially nothing (like me unwittingly spawning a wendigo in a bandit camp when I had nothing but an old hatchet)  and can easily get stuck in terribly frustrating death loops that will make you want to rage quit. 

The recovery system is likewise infuriating. Sleep, fight die. Wake up, sleep, sleep more. buff. fight. die. repeat the whole process a thousand times. Be prepared to sleep A LOT. for a "realistic" survival game you sleep an impossible amount because the game takes away most of your health bar after every death. I found this VERY tedious. 

And on top of all this, the game just feels ... empty. You wander a world that has the very occaisional mob and no map marker and when you finally find something in the wild it kills you and you have to scramble around the whole map trying to find it again, only to die...again. 

I gave it a serious go in the hopes it would start to get better as rewards trickled in from hard-scrabble dungeon crawls. They don't. I thought I would get better at the clunky combat... I didn't. Turns out, after some research, the way to get good is to cheese most things with bleeding or environment, or lay 15 traps down and watch the stupid AI walk through it. It's just poor design at the end of the day. Skip this one, please. You deserve better for your time.
its the worst game you ever played until its the best game you ever played. then it gets bad again, but you will like it this time.

Outward: A Masterclass in Respecting "Vision" More Than Players

Outward is a game that is deeply in love with its own philosophy, unfortunately at the total expense of the person playing it. While the developers at Nine Dots Studio claim to offer a "hardcore" survival experience, the reality is a product that feels less like a rewarding challenge and more like a series of lazy development shortcuts disguised as "immersion."

The "Mystery" of Incompetence
The most glaring issue is the game's pathological refusal to explain its own systems. There is a fine line between "no hand-holding" and "failing to explain core mechanics," and Outward leaps over that line. You are routinely punished for not knowing "key elements" that the game never bothered to teach you—like the fact that you’ve accidentally wandered into a high-level DLC zone scaled for end-game builds, or that specific enemies have nonsensical hitboxes. It’s not a test of skill; it’s a test of whether or not you have the Wiki open on a second monitor, which is just a sign of poor game design.

A World That’s Empty, Not "Vast"
The "adventure" aspect of the game is consistently undermined by a total lack of reward for exploration. In a game like Elden Ring or Morrowind, venturing off the beaten path leads to unique lore, powerful artifacts, or meaningful encounters. In Outward, you will likely spend twenty minutes jogging across an empty, procedurally-dead-feeling landscape only to find a chest containing a handful of silver and some scrap metal. The "risk vs. reward" balance is completely broken; the risk is permanent defeat and hours of backtracking, while the reward is often a joke.
Gear Dependency vs. Actual Growth
Unlike a proper RPG where your character grows stronger through experience, Outward features zero internal progression. You are a static set of numbers entirely dependent on gear and silver. If you don't have the right boots or a specific weapon, you are effectively a wet paper bag. This creates a frustrating loop where you can't get stronger without exploring, but you can't explore because everything kills you in one hit. Without a leveling system, there is no "natural" way to overcome a challenge other than grinding for cash to pay a trainer—making the game feel more like a bureaucratic chore than a heroic journey.

Final Verdict
Outward feels like it was developed by people who think "suffering" is a substitute for "depth." It is a clunky, poorly explained, and often disrespectful waste of time that punishes player curiosity rather than rewarding it. If you value your time and want a game that actually respects the "adventure" genre, look elsewhere.

[b]First of all, thank you for respecting the intelligence of your audience enough to not force-feed them. Things like no quest compass, vague journal entries, little to no hand-holding, landmark based navigation, no dungeon maps, [u]faction gameplay[/u], [u]meaningful and impactful equipment progression[/u] are all [u]GREAT[/u] things. Please never change things like these in your games. Also, thank you for releasing this on Steam. I wouldn't be playing right now if it was an Epic Store exclusive.[/b]

I think the game gives a very bad first impression in terms of gameplay. and that a lot of people (myself included) skipped the tutorial that would have made sliding into the world a little smoother, thus opening up possibilities it offers sooner. 

The world design being as spread out as it is, especially in that first few miles radius was a misstep by the devs, but I understand its function. The world itself becomes a hostile entity that you must learn how to most efficiently combat with your survival skills, armed with you weapons of upgraded hiking gear - sleeping bag, firestarting equipment, fur tent - portable alchemy set, and knowledge of formulas and recipes that mean you never have to return home if you don't want to. [b]The game tries to nail a sense of going on an adventure, and despite how poorly that may be conveyed, it actually does the whole adventurer sim thing better than most any other game I can think of.[/b] Once you feel on top of your game in the wilderness, I feel exploration really starts to open up, and the points of interest you have to discover become more plentiful and dense because of you ability to adeptly navigate your surroundings. Likewise, you start finding more interesting and valuable rewards at a quickening pace both on the field and in dungeons.

Speaking of dungeons, I like the tight, dank, dark feeling they impart. Their winding, disorienting nature is a positive in my eyes, and one of the most unique aspects of the game. I can see how they will piss a lot of people off, but they actually feel like dungeons, which is pretty cool. I enjoy the vital role that light source plays in them. You'll also find some really interesting things tonally and aesthetically in them. There is some nice environmental storytelling going on there, and it makes me want to find out more about this strange, warped, apocalyptic world. There's also cool things like gem activited doors that lead to optional parts of dungeons with nice surprises to reward the adamant player with.

Equipment progression is slow to begin with, but you start to feel the effects of every upgrade in huge ways once you get rolling. This is one of the most comparable aspects of the game to the Gothic games, though it reminds me of most of Monster Hunter, both in how tied to character progression it is, and how you end up crafting some of the best gear from the parts of your foes and surrounding environments.

As someone who has played a fair amount of this already, I'd say it'd be easy to write it off as an empty world full of grinding, but after a good full day of play, I just don't think that's the case. There is a lot of great things this game offers that will be missed because people will write it off in the first few hours, and honestly, that is the developer's fault. The game simply isn't for everyone because of this, but after sticking with it, its charm has revealed itself to me, and it has become a game that is for me. The way it all comes together is really like nothing I've ever played, and it's got me hooked. I want to join a faction and explore the whole mysterious world.

To address the challenge and death system from my perspective: I've mostly enjoyed it and appreciate how unique of an experience it can bring. There are apparently 90 death instances, and depending on what happens one can lead to another and you can find yourself in some sticky situations because of it. The problem is that so far, even when the worst has befallen me, I've still ended up with all my equipment, just injured and in need of time for rest. Or is this a problem? Really, when you think about, what you're losing is time and immediate location progress, which is just a modified and slightly more challenging version of save scumming. If you wake up close enough to where you were fighting, there's a chance you could run back even after resting to finish off your wounded opponent. But there is also a chance that by the time you return your opponent, they will have recovered and gathered allies again.

Overall, after thinking about it for awhile, I think I really like the system and have had fun with it. It's kind of a modified Souls game bonfire system, except more varied, random, and interesting when it works out. For people who think the game is too easy, start venturing into some of the more dangerous areas, and once or if you die, compare it to how your experience would have differed if you had save scummed the situation. I think you'll find the game just as challenging, or even more so with the added risk of dropping your pack for battle in a place that'll be hard to get to again. I feel like if there are more timed quests in the future, this could become even more of an interesting mechanic. I like how different it is, yet familiar, from how a lot of games handle death states.

[u]Also, amazing soundtrack! Great job Jean-Francois Racine. Just beautiful.[/u]

I love this game.  Perhaps it's my favorite.

The combat might feel busted and unfair at first, but it really isn't.  It's just different from games that have similar looking combat.  It can take a long time to learn, but once you do, it becomes predictable and manageable,  Even the weakest enemies can still be deadly if you aren't paying attention, though.

This is not a deep story-based RPG, nor is it a grand exercise in character development.    Outward is about the adventure. I admire a developer for staying true to a creative decision, in that this is a game where you are meant to scramble around to survive, explore, discover, and make your own way.

You aren't intended to be a legendary warrior with insane weapons, you are very human scramble around in a scarce world to stay fed, rested, sheltered, dry, warm, watered, and so forth. Listen to people and pay attention to your surroundings. Look where you're going as there's no fast travel or map markers. It's a great idea!

The game breaks down however in that it is extremely possible to get into negative feedback loops. Horrendous stealth mechanics, bad AI path finding/seeking, broken combat, etc all lead to an excruciating experience.

If you die, you're stripped of your critical items and dumped or imprisoned somewhere. You wake up with some combination of: delirious, starving, parched, exhausted, bleeding, wet, freezing, confused, weakened, etc. Now you have no source of food/water/bedroll etc and you're seriously at the bottom of a steep slope. Do you brave the wilderness with no light source and try to make it back to the main town? Or do you gut it out, and pray that going back into the bandit camp or whatever will help you find your lost gear, food, water and tent. Do you sprint for 10 minutes through the wilderness and hope a wild animal doesn't get ya? Or do you sprint into the enemy encampment and hope somehow you blindly stumble into your gear? You'll die 11 times whatever you decide and continue into the death spiral.

By the time you've spent 2 more hours and crawled out of whatever gameplay/resource/afflictions pit your previous death caused... you're fed again, found your backpack, had a good sleep, and are not thirsty any more... you're walking along and idk an arrow hits you out of nowhere and you're right back at the bottom of the pit. Items gone, afflicted with 3 statuses, nothing but salt water and angry dogs nearby.

Good luck.

I get what they were going for, but it's not fun.

And the worst, the WORST aspect of it all is that the game mechanics that you NEED are kinda broken or janky. Stealth is super broken to the point that I don't even get how it got out of QA. Enemy AI and pathing is so crude and it stands out like a sore thumb. You quickly get boxed into a corner and die again because even though it's pitch black at night, you're behind boxes blocking line of sight, you're crouching and nowhere near a patrolling enemy's route, suddenly he is magnetized exactly to your spot and "decides" to patrol over.

It's more exhausting to play than anything. If the devs wanted to philosophically push the gameplay experience into the harshness and realities of being human, they needed to shore up the aspects of the game that support the player in having that experience, not just hone the game play aspects that cripple, impair, and time waste.

Combat is trash. The last hope to overcome the cruel world is to bash in the skulls of the ones that just killed you, using gamer skill. But rolling doesn't register most of the time. The AI blocking is basically invincibility. Your attacks whiff constantly no matter how cleverly you position yourself and time your shots. But the AI can crush you into a human ragdoll bag of bones out of nowhere with an animation-teleport power shot.

Just no to all of it.

[b]TL:DR[/b] Having played through all 3 campaigns, played multiple styles, and done I believe every dungeon in the game. I think this is a great game if you have a friend to play it with. I do believe it would be very hard to enjoy solo. However, playing with my buddy we both liked it more than Skyrim. Sorry this got kinda long but I want people to know what they're getting into with Outward and how I think it can best be enjoyed.

[b]Suggestions to succeed in Outward:[/b]
[list]
[*] Play with a friend
[*] The combat feels dark soulsy but its not! There are no invincibility frames! If you try and roll through an attack you’re going to have a bad time
[*] If you want to do a magic build do some research as the magic system is complicated. It can be very powerful but some skills are underwhelming.
[*] Get the skills that let you move faster and reduce your stamina drain for running. (See No Fast Travel in Cons section)
[*] Do some research on the wiki and plan your build. You need strong weapons with attributes like bonus damage, bleeding, poison, fire, etc. The basic weapons you get from merchants won’t cut it once you start seeing stronger enemies.
[*] By planning your build you have something to work towards: weapons, armor, backpacks, skills
[/list]

[b]Magic[/b] As I said the magic system is complicated and here's why. All of the spells are combinations of each other.
[b]Examples:[/b] 
[list]
[*] The first spell you get is Spark which does basically nothing. However, cast the fire rune on the ground and stand in it and spark becomes fire balls. 
[*] Weapon enchantments. Cast the cold boon, now you can enchant your weapon with ice, another spell would also allow you to shoot ice blasts from this enchanted weapon..
[/list] 

[b]Builds[/b]
You can really make any build work if you put some planning into it. Every play through we did an entirely different build. Different weapons, armor, skills, and backpacks.
Example builds my friend and I did:
[list]
[*] Me with an axe of bleeding and shield. Buddy using magic and a pistol 
[*] Me with poison bow and arrows. Buddy with heavy armor and 2 handed axe
[*] Me with a light magic build (flame thrower) and  lightning spear. Buddy with a rogue type build
[/list]

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list] 
[*] The graphics are decent with some areas being absolutely gorgeous
[*] The campaign is fun and the story is interesting.
   NOTE: People say the story isn’t that good. It actually is pretty good but if you do not play all 3 campaigns you will not understand what happens. We played 1 faction and had a ton of questions! The next campaign answered most of the questions.
[*] Tons of armors / weapons / builds you can do. Lots of ways to customize your setup for your play style.
[*] Tons of dungeons. From small 1 room dungeons to a few massive dungeons that will get you lost.
[*] Lots of different enemy designs! The lightning desert shark may be one of the coolest I have seen in a long time.
[*] Lots of different areas and environments to prepare for. Is it snowing / desert? Each of these will have their own challenges.
[*] The world is rather massive and fun to explore. There are a lot of dungeons that are not on the maps.
[*] Crafting system for food / potions / drinks / weapons / armor is all in game. You don’t have to buy the recipes if you look them up.
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b] Most of this is just some quality of life improvements. Little bit of bug fixing and some finessing of mechanics. I doubt the mechanics will be changed but I would love to see a part 2 with this list fixed.
[list]
[*] NO FAST TRAVEL! This is probably the biggest complaint. The world is large and depending on where you are and where you are going it can easily take you 10 to 30 minutes running between places. If we could just pay one of the caravan merchants to travel with them between towns this would be a MASSIVE improvement to the game.
[*] There are some bugs no denying that. In general my friend and I hit very few game breaking bugs. Example being with my Archer build, I found if I held the right mouse button to ADS instead of just clicking it and then attempted to fire. My guy would glitch out and be unable to shoot arrows. I would have to leave the game and rejoin to fix it. I think in total we only saw about 3 bugs that required us to restart the game / session.
[*] There were some other random bugs we would see like the UI would glitch or something would happen. Typically we just found these funny and not really a problem.
[*] Load time bug: This was probably the most annoying bug. We only saw it once when I was the host but we saw it more frequently with my buddy. I think it may just be his internet but we’d sometimes have load time takes a few minutes. I think this is because NOTHING ever disappears from the game. If you just drop 100 items on the ground and come back months (in game time) later they’re still sitting there. Same with bodies of enemies you kill.
[*] There is definitely some desync issues! This again may be due to friend hosting and bad internet. But there were a few occasions where I picked up my bag and he could still see it on the floor. He could LITERALLY take my equipment off of me… If this was someone you don’t know trying to troll you they could literally strip you naked...
[*] The combat is good but it could use some finessing. It feels dark soulsy but the lack of i-frames will trick you into getting yourself killed until you learn. Same with getting knocked down. If an enemy just keeps swinging they can kill you before you’ll ever be able to get up or roll away.
[*] The magic system is complicated and I think could use a bit of a rework.
[*] Magic: You can get a number of rune spells that do nothing on their own but cast together can do awesome stuff. They literally don’t tell you the combinations as far as I saw. However, my buddy used this skill set to great affect! He just had to memorize what combination did what.
[*] Magic: The chakram spells are very underwhelming from our experience due to very limited range. If these had a longer range I think it would be far more useful.
[/list]
