Spend three hours trying to cross the swamp but every time you get defeated you get rescued to the far side of the map, or wake up in a bandit camp, or wake up back at the inn in town (and they've taken money from your pocket to pay for it)

Fish up boots

Get lightning-punched by a mantis shrimp

Die from frostbite in front of a campfire because it takes time for your body temperature to return to normal and you're still freezing to death while you oh-so-gradually warm up

Run out of arrows

Spend all your money on reagents needs to cast spells and then get ganked from behind and die anyway

Get your house repossessed in your first hour of playing because the HOA says your rent is overdue and they don't accept "it sank to the bottom of the sea" as an excuse

Oh my god you guys I love this game so much, I can't believe I didn't know about it until now.  It's so amazing.  This is wonderful.  :D

Ate dirt for the first ten hours, twenty more later and I'm crumpling bandits like tissue paper with a ten foot tall hammer. Makes you feel like weak trash until you don't, live your own Hero Arc and tussle until you're a real warrior. Then wear shell armor and make your own fun smacking troglodytes back to the stone age they came from.

Not for the faint of heart. You're going to struggle, but it makes your victories taste all the more delicious.

The number one thing I will say about this game is that you're just some random dude who has to pay rent. That's why there is no level system and why you get stomped by a comically large shrimp. The only meaningful progression in this game is the knowledge you acquire about your enemies and the world, and the gear you find on your travels. The game doesn't get easier, you just get better at it and that is why I love the game. If you think this game is for you then just jump in because this game isn't for everyone and the reviews show as much.

Be warned - not a real co-op game. You "host" a game but your friends that play with you get no quest experience, no quest rewards, no learned skills from NPCs. They are just there as "helpers" in your world.

Bought this game for local co-op, but it seems the split-screen partner does not receive any of the quest rewards, including the skills and items, thus rendering this game useless for co-op. Refunded.

This is one of THE best RPG games ever made of ALL time.

Mana and magic are entirely unique mechanics in this game, you don't start a mage, you need to pilgrimage to the mage mecca and exchange total health points for mana. This is really sick.

You don't just cast spells, you acquire sigils and cast them in combos to cast spells, kinda like arks fatalis but without drawing with a mouse.


Combat is unforgiving, punishing, you need to eat, drink, set up camp, sleep, cook, etc. 

if you fail to dispatch bandits they can capture you and bring you to their prison cells.

they can rob you, take your stuff and now you're back to square one.

The only thing this game is missing is reliable fast travel systems and/or mounts. There is NO reason someone should be walking across these maps more than once, but you will have to, and you do it on foot.

and because of this, EVERY time i play thru this game; I farm for a pearlbird mask and mastertrader garbs. Because these are the only armor items that give you total % increase in movement speed, and thus these are the defacto best items in the game.

i dont use other armor, because they dont allow you more movementspeed. I don't want less movement speed because this game forces you to walk everywhere. 

This becomes a problem in CoOp too because your buddy isn't gonna get lucky with the games loot tables and drop a pearl mask early for them too, so now you have one guy unable to keep up with the other, because the movementspeed is that broke. it will disrupt your co op partners gameplay, and it will funnel you into the distinct decision to use these same items as well.. because.. well.. you don't want to move slow.

this is the ONLY problem this game has. there is a small amount of clunk to the game, but not enough to disrupt the experience of the game itself.

Because of this movement speed issue i'm gonna have to give it an 8/10. 

if this game got horse dlc or an update that added mounts or town fast travel for a price, it'd be an instant 10/10. but due to the spacious scale of the maps, it sours the journey from A to B after awhile.

tldr; this is a must play for RPG enjoyers, Co Op game fans, this is one of the most unique RPGs ever made.

[h1] I love this game. [/h1]
But that wasn't the question Steam asked, it asked if I can recommend this game. And there is a very high chance that you, dear reader, will not like this game.

You probably won't like that the "tutorial" level barely teaches you the basic controls, and skips over many important topics.

You probably won't like that the game starts by leaving you shipwrecked with nothing, and quickly moves along to giving you a time limit to pay off a debt that neither you through gameplay nor the character you play earned.

You probably won't like that joining up with one of the factions the game provides is not an equal challenge, as some factions are difficult to even reach.

You probably won't like that the incredibly limited inventory space encourages you to forgo picking up everything you find, or at least dropping things as your pack fills up. And on the subject, you probably won't like that combat expects you to take the time to drop your bag and fight without its contents.

You probably won't like that you get only 8 quickslots, which are used for everything from swapping weapons to using consumables to performing skills and spells, and doing any of these (especially skills) through the menu is not the most viable in combat. And while I'm talking about it, you probably won't like that using items in combat is already difficult with how long it takes to so much as drink a potion, much less apply a bandage.

You probably won't like how limited long-term storage is, starting the game with only a stash chest that's near literally in the corner of the world, forcing you to live out of your backpack for a large portion of the game.

You probably won't like that you can't stockpile useful foods, both because of the weight limit and because even foods meant for preservation like jerky won't last long (excepting Travel Rations, but those aren't useful as [i] food). [/i]

You probably won't like the lack of a conventional leveling system, meaning that your only character upgrades come from acquiring more powerful equipment or finding and paying trainers for skills, with the trainers that have full skill trees to learn becoming incredibly expensive for more than the most basic skills. And on the subject, you probably won't like that you can only fully advance 3 skill trees.

You probably won't like that money is hard to earn [i] especially [/i] in the early game and that carrying your money with you not only puts it at risk if your health drops to 0, but also weighs down your bag (and again, storage is limited for a long time).

You probably won't like that there's no conventional fast travel with this game, expecting you to walk through dangerous environments for long periods of time to get from city to city, having to be prepared for everything from wild beasts to hostile temperatures.

You probably won't like that you don't start with magic, requiring you to go through a dangerous dungeon just to get access to it, and you have to trade your health and stamina to acquire mana. And on the subject, you probably won't like that there are very few spells which are directly useful, with most requiring you to use spells in combination to produce useful effects (remember the limited quickslots?).

You probably won't like that a portion of your health and stamina get burned as they get depleted, temporarily reducing your maximum values. And while sleeping is the easiest way to restore burned health and stamina, it comes at the cost of burning your mana instead.

You probably won't like that upon dying, there are incredibly varied consequences that range from being inconvenienced by waking up in the starting town after several days have passed to literally being taken prisoner and separated from all your gear until you find a way out of your situation. And in addition, you will frequently be teleported to unfamiliar parts of the region upon dropping to 0 HP, forcing you to find landmarks that you recognize to find your way again.

You probably won't like that there are no mechanics for identifying how strong your opponents are, instead relying on visual language to display how tough an enemy is. You can guess a person in metal armor with imposing weapons or a large, horrible looking beast that sprays particle effects are likely going to be challenging, but there's no way of knowing just how tough they are until you engage them.


But all these things, while often frustrating, create an unrivaled sense of exploration. I feel like someone trying to survive my forays into the world, living out of my pack as I discover various locations, dungeons, people, trainers, and so on. I'll often be out for (in game) days at a time before returning home, trying to decide what to keep and what to toss and looking for a safe place to camp so I'm not stuck taking twice as long to rest. I like the feeling of finding what you can out in the wild to survive, using a campfire and a cooking pot to turn ordinary ingredients into useful food. I like that I'm encouraged to explore in order to find new equipment and meet new trainers in order to get stronger. I even like that several quests are time limited, as that adds a sense of pressure and immersion when I fail to get somewhere on time since I spent too much time resting to restore my resources (and died a few times on the way, leading to even more resting). I spent over 20 hours in this game without even joining a faction, a requirement to progress the game's quests, just because I was having so much fun exploring all the different regions. I even got myself into a really sticky situation by traveling to an area that was far too strong for me without the travel rations to get back home, which meant I had to find or make some more before I was allowed to leave.

To sum it up, this game is not for everyone. Not even close. But if this game is for you, you'll love it.

To be clear: This game is not for everyone. It requires a different mindset when facing it.
I do not mean it in the elitist way of "you're not good enough" or "only for true gamers".

I pirated this game years ago, and I rage-uninstalled it. I re-downloaded it again, played with my partner, and the same thing happened. We both ended up so frustrated that I uninstalled it again.
A few months ago, I actually bought it as a way of forcing myself to give it a try, this time solo.

And for the first 8 hours or so... I've suffered. I have restarted countless times, died more than I have died playing any Dark Souls game, uninstalled and reinstalled it twice. It IS a hard game, THAT is why it requires a change of mindset:

1. Deaths are NOT deaths. You can not die in this game, you're always knocked out and then... "Something" happens. Bandits find you and enslave you, wild beasts drag you to their lair, a friendly hunter finds you and brings you to heaven, or even the good old deus ex machina of feeling a goddess' call and feeling reinvigorated. You WILL lose stuff, I have lost over 800 silver coins to bandits once!
Deaths are not a punishment per-se, they're just small pauses in whatever you were doing, and you might even be closer to that location, or find some cool loot while trying to escape, or earn some money in prison as the most efficient slave until they release you for it. You will die, it will be unfair for some time, but do not give up. Everything you can lose (bandits take your armor or your money) can be fixed by either taking those items back from a stash or not carrying your money in the wildlands, but leaving it at a safe spot.

2. The combat is clunky, slow and deadly. I do not recommend playing defensive, nor I recommend magic for a first playthrough. But this is not Bloodborne, Sekiro or Elden Ring. Stop, block and dodge your enemies' attacks. Learn their patterns, when you can punish, and learn to attract enemies one by one to not get overwhelmed. Use fences, abuse the AI to confuse it and deal with the combats slowly. Managing your stamina is crucial, so don't be afraid to lock-off the camera from the enemy and walk away while recovering stamina slowly.

3. The consumables are important. Of course, save the potions and powerful stuff for when you're deep inside a dungeon, or for a boss, but use whatever you have to make your life easier. Traps, items that infuse your weapon, the environment will also give you what you need in certain parts of the game like Dark Souls 1 does with the temporary curses to attack the ghosts. Something like that. Learn what recipes and ingredients give you health regeneration (or look it up on the internet as I did because I got frustrated) and craft a hell lot of bandages, meat, vegetables... This is Breath of The Wild now, enjoy.

4. Leveling. There's no leveling. Your character can learn skills from NPCs that train you, as long as you have money, and you can get stuff like some more health, stamina, magicka and some special moves, but there is not experience nor levelling system.

5. Weapons. This is how you will know you're ready for bigger tasks. Weapons can have different effects, but I focused more on just bonking hard and damaging the enemies' "posture" more than their health. Check how much impact a weapon has on the enemy's posture and abuse the stun system. If you learn their patterns and can stun them frequently, you can take down any enemy even with a low-damage weapon.

6. Armors. There are two kind of stats for armors: Elemental resistance (pretty self explanatory) and Protection. What you're gonna need to go for is Protection. Most armors do NOT have a Protection value, only elemental resistance, so you'll be getting three hitted easily by small enemies. My tip is follow the mission that the blacksmith gives you at the initial town and get the Blue Sand armor set. It will let you start fighting and exchanging hits even with some minor bosses, survive longer and, therefore, earn more money and get the stuff going.

This has been my experience summarized. Right now, I am enjoying and exploring the world. It is true it's a bit empty, but that's only when you kind of... Already did everything a region has to offer. Once I changed the way I was going through this game and started acting cautious and smart like the game requires from you, it is a really enjoyable ARPG with survival elements.

Most people get into this game not understanding/knowing how difficult the game will actually be, which explains the more recent mixed reviews. It's a lot of people buying from sale and getting mad that the game isn't as forgiving as something like Dark Souls with its death mechanics. It's not, you're going to be put at like 25% hp at the bottom of a cave that's filled to the brim with enemies. Good luck getting out, because it will take you like 2 hours to figure it out. 

[b]This is not a game that rewards blindly tackling a situation.[/b]

If you go somewhere without a game plan, you will die. If you get overwhelmed, you will die. If you get cornered, you will die. Even with some of the best gear in the game, you will die. Imagine if you will, Dark Souls' incredible combat but you're drunk. That's about how combat flows in this game. Drunk Dark Souls. It's slower, more methodical, easier to make mistakes, and very easy to take hits. You move slowly, as this is a slow paced game. Coming into this game you must realize, the first zone you're in? You're going to be there for a while. Probably 4+ hours. Not because you're stuck there, but because you don't know what to do. And that's okay. There are tons of people willing to help you along your journey who want you to succeed. This game truly is a treasure, but you need to get through that initial first rough patch.

The story in this game is actually solid enough to stand its own ground. The game starts off with you coming back from a trip overseas, but you were caught in a shipwreck. Go through the basic bare-bones easy baby tutorial, and you finally arrive home. Where you're immediately given a 150 silver debt and a week to pay it or you lose your home. Right off the bat, you're in for a rough time. You need to figure out how to make 150 silver in a week, pay off your house before that happens or you lose it. Forever. You cannot reobtain it back. Oh by the way, all quests have a time-limit in this game. This isn't just central to the house, but every single quest. If you do not complete them within the time limit, your rewards change. Outcomes change. Entire storylines change. I highly recommend not going in blindly, looking up what to expect and what type of armor you want to obtain. Saw one dude make a review after 'losing' their blue sand armor in the Vendavel Foretress. You can get it back. [b]YOU WILL ALWAYS BE ABLE TO OBTAIN YOUR GEAR BACK UNLESS YOU ARE A HARDCORE CHARACTER OR YOU HAVE DIED WITH A VERY SPECIFIC SKILL THAT MOST OF YOU WILL NOT OBTAIN BECAUSE IT CAUSES PERMANENT DEATH[/b] This is why I say do not go in blind. If you can't find your gear and you're naked, look up the zone you're in to figure out how to get your gear back. You aren't going to make it far naked and afraid.

This game will not be an easy time. It's a viciously difficult game until you understand the game's rules and take advantage of the one thing you have over a programmed AI: You can lay traps. If you lay enough traps around a boss that isn't aggroed, you can instantly kill them. You can prepot to high heaven, eat all the food buffs. There's no reason for you to go into a fight without any buffs. Realistically, you want some kind of stamina regen buff and healing buff at all times. Cook some raw meat and eat gabberries in the first zone. In other zones, find what is available to you. Black Marsh has Marshmelons, which are quite powerful for stamina regeneration.

Stop giving the game a bad review because you didn't know what you were getting into. Co-op works fine, you don't share skills. It encourages both of you to take different story paths. You keep your gear, inventory, money etc. Just go join your friends world with your new gear that you spent hours obtaining and smash the early game. You can do that yourself if you want too, there's tons of guides of how to transfer gear to other characters. Some items don't come til near the end of the game, can't use them for long if you get them so late. Send them to a new character. Be overpowered in the first area, look at how far you have come and see the raw power you have achieved. After that you may start to appreciate what the game for what it is, and being upset that it isn't the new dark souls of dark souls.

This is a game designed for a specific type of player. If you can appreciate a true challenge, hard save settings, hard survival settings then this is for you. It is a rare gem of a game that rewards the player for meticulous planning and clever thinking. Combat is great and meaningful, gameplay is superb. 
I shall give one example: 
I was scouting south/east of starting city at night, darkness total, music ambient, I decided to turn my lantern on as I could see the outline of a cave opening.... I was attacked by 4 hyenas from behind. killed one, knocked out by the others.... I thought that was it... no it wasn't. a loading screen came up and the writing was something like this (from memory) "You awake to the noise of flesh and bone being torn apart and devoured, you look right and see a half eaten leg beside you, you realise the hyenas have saved you for a later dinner...." I got up, realised only one hyena had stayed behind to feast picked up a shiny iron sword from the poor chap being eaten (now have first iron sword) absolutely battered that mother****** went outside and another 5 hyenas were just off to the right, so I snuck left and made my slow bloody, stamina depleted crawl back to my home Village THIS WAS AN EPIC EXPERIANCE!

I am right at start of the game, basic weapons, leather armour, primitive backpack, no magic. Honestly I am a hardcore RPG single player gamer and this is a masterpiece, a welcome experience when most games hold your hand and make the whole journey about following markers and instant fixes.

Looking forward to seeing the rest of the developers hard work.

Roll on the rest of this epic journey.

This game is top-shelf. Is it perfect? No. But it contains creativity and focus to deliver an experience and vision that is unique in "recent" gaming memory. There is nothing else like Outward, in the best way possible.

This game asks you to pay attention. It wants you to act like an adult. Its NPCs aren't fooled by leaving the area and immediately returning. You can't patronize your way into everyone's good books. The story is much, much richer than you first realize. Your first character will barely have a grasp of the world - because the world has several competing factions you might not even realize are really, truly competing in a living world. 

There is a magic casting system that is second to none. You can enchant weapons for certain scenarios, bring different load outs based on the locations or enemy types. You can line a hallway with devious traps and not engage in combat at all. You can do it ALL in co-op with another player, which unlocks even more play styles and possibilities for adventure.

The artwork and sound is astounding. The story/lore is wonderful - enchanting, and unique. Nothing is quite like Outward. The sights and art and sounds are not found anywhere else. Sure, aspects of the game aren't perfect due to the obviously MASSIVE level of ambition by Nine Dots - but they did a wonderful job getting MOST of it across. Yeah, fine, you can't "see" the war happening, but you can talk about how it is affecting different factions and different peoples. You play a pivotal role in many different outcomes to the world, or you ignore them and they play out with none of your participation. The game truly wants to immerse you in its world and for you to invest in it. And you are rewarded handsomely for doing so with awesome dungeons and rewards, encounters, and loot.

Get Outward. If you play Outward and dislike it, you're wrong and you should just play longer. I promise you unless you're using guides or following walkthroughs you can roll you're 10th character and see sights in this game game or discover play style you never even imagined were possible.

The concept of the game is top-tier. The idea of an action RPG with intense survival mechanics and realistic progression deeply resonates with me. However, a game that prides itself on difficulty MUST ensure that the combat is extremely refined which is simply not the case here. Enemies frequently move in ways that defy physics, and hit detection is bizarrely inconsistent.

Incredibly tedious. Combat tries to emulate dark souls, but there is no impact to your attacks. Tried fighting a dagger wielding bandit with a two-handed blunt weapon and the guy didn't even blink when I hit him. This means that the combat is closer to skyrim, where you just have to out-dps your enemy. Sure, you can block but there's no point because you can't take advantage of openings. 

For example, I fought a guy wielding an iron sword while I had a shield and a mace. I held my shield up to block and when he struck it, I immediately swung my mace to punish his swing. But It was pointless, because even though my attack connected, he didn't stagger or flinch or react at all to it. Dodging works great, sure, but you have to attack eventually. And when you attack, they attack THROUGH your attack so what's the point?

You take an MMORPG, take out the players and levels and add survival elements to the game that can kind of resembles Rust's survival in terms of the basics: Eat and drink.  Except you need to sleep in this game and you can get varying illnesses in the game.  Some of which can actually evolve into a more acute state of illness, like infections can get worse with time if not treated right away.  This makes the game pretty painful for newer players and seems like a totally tedious game, but once you get into it, you can actually enjoy having to prepare for such events.
         Another thing some may want to note is the combat.  I did mention its a lot like an MMORPG, but its combat is far from it.  The combat is painful and slow, it is something that will make some people not even want this game, but it realistic in terms of the risk at hand.  It is EXTREMELY difficult to handle multiple enemies at once in this game as they will aim to flank you and will relentlessly poke you if you don't have enough distance between you and your enemies.  Let alone if you are in a 1v1 scenario, you need to manage your stamina constantly, as it pretty much is consumed upon every action and if you find yourself with no stamina, you find yourself having a bad time.  This makes the point of preparation before venturing out or combat essential as you can buff yourself before hand like other games and you can set ACTUAL traps.  Some games might have like a bear trap or something, but this game takes it somewhat a level up.  
         You get two trigger devices as far as I know: the pressure plate and the tripwire.  These seem pretty basic to use, and they are, what makes them amazing is what you can use as the weapon for the trap.  For the tripwire you have the traditional spikes that can harm your enemy and inflict "pain" on them, reducing physical resistance by 25%, or you can use certain material items from enemies as the weapon device, such as the "assassin tongue" which does high physical damage and can slow and bleed an enemy (correct me if I am wrong).  And there are no limit to the traps you can place, making traps nearly essential when you know a tough fight is ahead as they give such an edge in combat.
        As far as the story goes, I quite like it myself, its actually a pretty fast paced one if you have the materials at hand for travelling a lot, otherwise you will be camped out for a bit in your home (if you have it) or in the wilderness until you can travel to the next area safely.  But basically the story can branch off in different directions depending faction you choose.  Kind of like Fallout really, but it makes for an interesting take on the game and if you like roleplaying in your games, which this game is good at, then you will probably enjoy the story as long as you stay intune with your character and the world around you.

The coop experience is super fun, be prepared to have a lot of arguments about loot, who is to blame for the party's death and "how the hell are we lost???". The early game is difficult and there's no holding hands so you must have patience to learn and even so brace yourself to be humiliated by common bandits every once in a while. Some features may be dealbreakers, like the insta save (similar to Dark Souls, so you must live with the consequences of your decisions) and the fact that player 2 in coop is more like a helper (the main quests are player 1 oriented and only them will receive the skills and unique items as rewards). All in all, Outward is a must buy on sale, the soundtrack alone is well worth it!

Writing a review after attempting to play this game multiple times over the course of the past four years. The first time I played it co-op, got a game breaking bug that one of the players got stuck. A year later, played co-op again, co-op character got deleted halfway through game. Just recently tried the game 02/2023, co-op friend disconnected and lost their inventory. I want to like the game but just to many game breaking bugs.
I wish the Devs could officially support 2-4 player coop with quest enabled for everyone.

What a game. 
No other game in recent memory, maybe since first Baldur's Gate i played on my pentium 3 made me truly feel like an adventurer as much as this one. You're not some messiah god come to life, destined for great things... No! You're a shmuck. You know nothing. You have a sword that you barely know how to use, ragged shirt, threadbare pants, some water, some bread, a "backpack" barely big enough to hold it all in and your determination. 

Then, you come through the gate out of the safety of the town, and all you have to go on is a quest to get a mushroom if you were lucky enough to find it. I didn't first time round.

And your adventure begins.

If you're hungry, buy food, hunt food, cook food, eat food or don't and you'll get debuffs.
If you're thirsty, drink water, but be careful the water might be dirty, it might even be dirty enough to give you diseases. 
If you're cold, find wood and make a campfire to get warm or get fur clothes to keep warm or sleep in fur tent.
If you're hot you have to drink water, in the desert you have to drink a lot of water and since it's a desert and water there is extremely rare you have to keep chuging just to keep the heatstroke at bay.

It sounds annoying as hell on paper (and apart from this one and subnautica i disliked every single survival game i tried) , but how all these things mesh together (like in subnautica) is, for me at least, amazingly atmospheric.
Your armor matters, your weapon matters, your backpack matters, your buffs matter, your potions matter, your food matters, your crafting skills matter, your lantern once you get it matters a lot, you need all the edge you can get.

No enemy is a pushover, no debuff is inconsequential, you can't just assassins creed your way through things with brain turned off. Use you head and overcome adversity. It's a great feeling.

I haven't spent that many hours on a single player game in forever and i'm not even done. If you want a game that makes you feel like you earned every little thing you got with your sweat and tears, try this game out. I did without expecting much and it's in my top 5 of all time. 

Bravo devs.

Outward - A TRUE diamond in the rough.

*TLDR* This game is a RPG with HEAVY survival elements, but it is NOT a survival game in the vein of rust, ark, subnatica, valhiem or anything like that. BUT to truly enjoy outward, you HAVE to go in with the right mindset, which means knowing that the game is slow paced, and is all about the journey, and properly preparing. It is very janky and has a obvious lack of budget but if you take the time to learn the games systems, there is NOTHING like it. I highly recommend watching a dozen or so outward tip videos on youtube shortly after trying the game. my full review explains why co-op made this game go from a 3/10 to an 11/10 for me

  
Let me start this review off by saying that I have over 400 hours on the PS4 version. - Which is by far the WORST version of this game overall.

This will be a bit of a longer review, but it is one that I think explains why this game is in my top 5 games of all time and how it came to be that game.

So I started following outward wayyyyyyyyyy back before the game ever came out when I saw a development video that included gameplay. Being that Bethesda games are my FAVORITE games of all time, a new open world RPG to scratch the itch was beyond welcome. The CEO of nine dots talked about how the game had a bunch of unique ideas such as careful preparing, managing your backpack, camping, crafting, making traps, and RITUALISTIC MAGIC. The three things that caught my attention the most was how you acquire magic by going through a dungeon and sacrificing some of your health and stamina for the magic pool in their placement, the preparation needed for combat with things like setting up traps or multiple steps needed to cast magic, and the SPLIT SCREEN CO-OP!!!! I was in awe and super eager!

So, fast forward to the day the game drops. I could not find a physical copy anywhere, including gamestop (they didnt even know what it was and said it wasnt in their system at all), so I resorted to just going digital on my ps4. the my surprise, the ps4 version was BAD, and had a ridiculous gap in quality, especially textures and lighting, from what I saw on the pre-release streams. I was bummed by played for a bit anyways. I had NO idea what I was doing, even as a RPG veteran and connoisseur. I quickly became frustrated and dropped the game. I tried multiple times but it never once clicked.

fast forward again to 2 years later, to the summer of 2021. I am now living with my girlfriend at the time, and in my long long wait for starfield or elder scrolls 6, I was in desperate need to get my sandbox open world RPG fix and I looked at outward again but with determination this time. I convinced my girlfriend to give it a shot with me (shes a pretty big gamer as is). But I KNEW she would drop the game immediately if I didnt figure it out first. So I started the game solo friday night, and just started figuring out stuff on my own. Saturday morning, she goes to work, and I hit up the old youtube beginners tips and tricks videos for like 6 or 8 hours. After learning so much on how to get started, I did just that and got myself set up with some money and gear and familiarized myself with the game. The next day, my girlfriend and I are both off of work, and I tell her that she needs to bear with the game because it WILL click (it already had started with me). and outward we went. by the end of the night, we were having a blast.

This summer of 2021 will go down as one of the best times of my life (and I was fortunate enough to have great summers with my friends growing up). My girlfriend and I played outward EVERY night for probably 2.5 or 3 months straight. We started staying up late and playing all day during the weekends. We quit cooking dinner and were ordering take out, delivery, or cooking super fast meals at home because we just wanted to keep playing. Obviously we kept going to work and taking care of all of life's needs, but in all of our free time at the house alone together, outward was what we were doing. We played through the base game and its DLCs, killed all the optional bosses, and collected the rarest gear we could find.

Fast forward once again to march of 2023. My girlfriend and I get engaged. A few weeks ago we were laying in bed and the topic of when we knew we wanted to get married to one another came up and we both agreed that the summer we played outward was one of those moments. We both agreed that we wanted to have thought kind of fun come up again at some point in our lives, and that we wanted to do it together. Obviously im not saying that we just want to play video games all day and eat like crap, but we realized just how much fun we could have together in those quiet moments at home. There are a lot of reasons why I love my fiance, but being able to sit down, have fun, and laugh is a special one that means a lot to both of us.

Outward is a very cool and fun game that you can play with your friends, but the way to co-op sets you up for preparing, strategizing, and sets you off on a true journey makes it something special. Outward is a game that requires true team work in co-op. 


Outward is something SPECIAL.


The mechanics of outward are what truly set it apart though. The way you have to prepare is its defining feature. its not just an adventure, its an adventure you make, and its challenges that you TRULY overcome by yourself. Not by "getting gud" (because of the stamina based combat) and not by grinding up your levels (there are no level ups!), but because everything you achieve to make yourself better comes from 1)knowledge on the players part and 2) The gear you earn or make and 3) the way you prepare for the challenge you know you will face. 

outward is not a immersive experience like a Bethesda game, you will DEFINITELY be looking at the META for this game, and you will be doing it a LOT. The story and lore are only to facilitate the game play. The game is all about exploring, getting you BUTT KICKED, and then going around, getting the gear you need, and coming back and either mopping the floor with the enemies, or barely scraping by, by the skin of your teeth.


if you try it and dont like it, i strongly suggest you think about what the game is, and isnt, watch some youtube videos on how to get some momentum, and even watch some of the videos from the dev talking about the type of game they were trying to make, and playing it that way, rather than playing it like every other rpg youve played, because its really doing something VERY different, even if it may not look that way from the outside. It is not skyrim, it is not the witcher, it is not a soulsike, it is not fable, it is not dragons dogma, it is not dragon age, it is not greedfall, it is OUTWARD and it is UNIQUE. 


please, i implore you to give this game a fair chance. it truly holds a special place in my heart.

Ideally, in 10 years time I'll be able to look back and say that this is an unplayable nightmare jank pile masquerading as a game, because people will have executed on it's core concepts much better. But if you'd asked me my hopes after playing Morrowind 10 years ago, I'd have said the same thing, and that hasn't happened. 

In the mean time, Outward has a lot of problems. It puts a bunch of largely artificial barriers between you when you first start and being 'allowed' to enjoy the game, by doing things like making you pay a (at that point) sigificant amount of money to learn basic crafting stuff (like, say, health and mana potions.) The balancing is poor (Mages start OP as hell because they can 1 shot everything and get progressively weaker by comparison as the game goes on because they take way more damage, Melee starts very weak because you rely on weapons and armor and there's very little of either that's any good available early on but ends up massively OP because you can stunlock basically everything in the game to death, shields and daggers are just hot garbage ect.,) the main quest is interesting in theory but isn't delivered super well, the quest timers in such a long game are (as always in long games) frustrating rather than fun (especially for a game so focused on exploration,) the graphics look straight off of an Xbox 360 in 2009 and the character models are even worse than that, and in general the game sets you up to fail at the start in a way that just feels awful to deal with, even if you know how to avoid it. 

So why the thumbs up? 
Well, if you can get past all of that (and there is a lot to get past) there's also a lot of good, and there's almost nowhere else to get it in a game that's been released in the last 20 years. Travel and navigation is an integral part of the game instead of just boring downtime between the interesting bits, the atmosphere they create with the primitive graphics is universally well done, the music is great, the combat works, the magic system is really, really cool, and in general the game respects your intelligence and abilities. It's way more than the sum of it's parts

Not scripted, not part of a quest, it just...happens, and it's magical.

Amazing Co-Op Souls-like/Skyrim/Survival type of game with some glaring issues, but can be 'solved'.

-I put over 50 hours into this playing with my bro, for the price i got it for on sale, that is definitely worth it even if it felt a little frustrating or monotonous at times. The main issue i have with this game probably is the walking sim aspect of it. You will spend a ton of time just walking from point a to b, and the fetch quests that this game likes to do sometimes doesn't help either. 

-That's why i highly recommend you get mods for this game, even just for that alone. Even with a Increased travelling speed mod, it still does feel like a chore, but it is significantly better and will extend meaningful gameplay instead of just walking. 
-Mods can fix a lot of the balancing and mechanics of this game aswell. Another crucial mod i recommend is some sort of meditate or sitting mod that regens your stats, or an extra quickslot mod, but those can be seen as too game breaking for some.

-Combat is actually pretty fun but is still janky. I went with a full on mage build with Hex (status effect buildup), Sigils (act like zones to cast strong spells from) and Rune Sage (imagine jutsu hand weaving from Naruto). Got to a point where i had a ton of mana reduction on my armor so i basically had infinite mana. My brother did a revolver/punching build which was pretty funny and did some crazy stagger. You have lots of options in this game for combat which is nice, and the survival mechanics are okay for the most part.

-Story was alright, didn't have much to say bad or good about it. I did Holy Mission questline, which is the best one to start off with imo. You are locked out of 3 other main questlines and have to do New Game to experience those stories. This is good for replayability but it also sucks to have to restart pretty much everything every time. It took us around 50 hours to complete with us taking our time but also having QoL mods. I stopped shortly after the main quest, as the DLC questline requires you to BUILD a goddamn CITY which requires a ton of grinding and gold farming.

-Music is pretty good actually i enjoyed the soundtrack, sound effects are decent, voice acting is kinda funny and bad at times tho. but who really cares

-I haven't mentioned it yet, but as most reviews point out: This game is ball crushingly hard at times. especially the first 10 or so hours. Hell i'd probably steal the "Prepare to Die" Tagline from Dark Souls and give it to this game. It was clear that this was a intentional design choice, because there is so many different death scenarios that it's kind of crazy.
-Early game is built different and it is really hard to get good gear, especially armor as even 50 hours into the game and my bro still hated the armor sets he was using. A lot of OP stuff is locked behind End/After game so that isn't great either, as is are no leveling up in this game, it is all based on skills you learn and gear you have. 
-It does drop off significantly near the mid/end I'd say (not counting DLC), which is pretty rewarding considering what you had to go to. Defintely watch a lot of youtube videos and tutorials for this game. Sheenshots was a W for my playthrough

-Overall, it is a really good co-op experience if everyone playing has some decent patience, and a lot of the major issues can be solved with mods (recommend R2modman easiest way to mod the game, remember to set the Beta build on steam to the mono branch). The highs are 9/10, and the lowest of lows are probably a 3/10 lol. Usually the game is a 7 or 8 i would say.

Definitely needs more recognition but also i would try to get this game on a good sale due to the issues. I got this for like less than 15 canadian.

I'm going to say this: I did not enjoy this game in the first 5 or so hours.

I did not enjoy the combat, the slow pace, the vast empty lands, the way no information was given to me at face value, NO FAST TRAVEL.

But at hour 10 or so, I started to see this masterpiece as what it really is: an RPG that punishes you if you don't prepare for the worst.

What I mean by being prepared is: getting supplies, getting the best equipment you can get, planning where to go next, predict what's going to happen and respond, do research on what kind of environment you're in, and always ALWAYS overpower yourself as much as you can. Because if you don't, the enemies will.

Combat is slow and clunky but it offers tangible tactics that can be used: consumables, traps, kiting, skills, passives, magic, buffs, debuffs, weaknesses, strengths... and most important of all - Running Away. Oftentimes, when you get killed in combat, it would mean you are not utilising any strategy or tactics. It's like going into a battlefield with a pea shooter but the only thing you're going to do is charge at the enemy who has better guns. It will obviously not end well.

Outward is more than just completing quests: it's about exploration and overcoming challenges. The map is not a friend. It is merely a guide. It shows important landmarks but they are most often generic names. Dungeons can be found scattered here and there but they're not shown because obviously these dungeons have never been explored before or has been left forgotten. You make your way yourself.

Honestly, the best part of me becoming addicted to this game is the fact that even if you get the best gears in the world, you can still get bodied easily, but at the same time you can also kill them as fast if you're utilising tactics and strategies.

This game has a lot of great aspects - the gear is cool, crafting is fun, and the scenery is beautiful. Multiplayer is easy to use too. Playing solo is really difficult as far as combat goes but it's great with another person. The reason my partner and I stopped playing it is because of the exceptionally long and boring travel times between quests. The maps are large and each quest seems to send you all the way across the map. Once you've cleared an area, you're just running forever before you reach your destination. If the game had included some kind of faster mount, like horses, or a fast travel system, or even paying a caravan some silver to transport you to the next destination then the game would be much more enjoyable.

So people did not lie - that Outward can be difficult.
Honestly, part of that is the unforgiving nature of the game as intended, part of that is the - let's face it - janky and outdated combat. It feels stiff and unresponsive at times, and I assume the devs intended that so it felt more 'realistic'. Sometimes, tho, it just feels clunky. I find myself just avoiding fights if I'm playing alone (or else spamming traps and lanterns and things of that nature).

But, aside from that, the game has quite a bit of charm to it. The survival mechanics are basic and honestly? I prefer that. No one needs to reinvent the wheel here, and accidentally stumbling upon new recipes through experimenting in crafting is actually a lot of fun. I've only just now entered the 'second area' in the overworld map and I feel like I've already discovered a lot.

Also, I get to play it with my best friend and he is very good at saving my butt when I run into the same trap for the third time and run out of bandages.

I'm so tired of fast, easy, cheap, dumbed-down game play that takes away from the experience for the sake of convenience. In that regard, this game is like a breath of fresh air. If you like a game that offers immersion and challenge, this one is definitely worth checking out!

I love that this game:
- focuses on exploration, survival, resource management, and preparedness; simply trekking through the wilderness is a major challenge of the game. It is not simply assumed that you reach your destination.
- doesn't hold your hand; it's challenging and requires you to use your head. charging blindly into an unknown situation is the surest way to fail.
- doesn't have quest markers, way points, fast travel, maps with player markers on them, and other immersion breaking short cuts; you have to figure out where you are, where you are going, how to get there, and what to look for, yourself. You will quickly become well acquainted with the game world in this way, making it feel more alive and relevant.
- has a game world, lore, story, and characters that are interesting, and that have been thought through and not simply slapped together.
- combat is dangerous, risky, and lethal, making it more rewarding when you are victorious. Think dark souls.

I stumbled over this game by accident in steam. I checked the screenshots and description and some reviews. I play games like divine divinity 2, baldurs gate, neverwinter, etc. i always long for games that i can look forward playing to, which immerse me enough to enjoy it.
I played Gothic 2 back in 2001 and it was til today for me one of the games with the fondest memories about immersion, exploration and fun. 

Much was reviewed about Outward already, but for me other factors than those made it a blast so far.

Immersion:
- you wear a fancy brimmed hat early on
- you cram stuff in your visible backpack.
-you can attach a lamp to it, which you have to refill when the oil is used up.
- you use a bedroll or a tent when you need to rest, which you have to lay out on the ground and pack back in when you're done. You can/will put a camp fire before it, when it is too cold so you wont freeze while sleeping or if you want to cook.
- dungeons are a mix of being too dark to go without a lamp/torch, which you hold in front of you like indiana jones and normal light.
- when you sneak and wear a light source, enemies will spot you much farther ahead.
- you can lay down campfires. You can put your kettle onto it, to cook fancier meals or you can put an alchemy-device on top of it to brew potions.
- you carry 2h-weapons with one hand over your shoulder while walking running, no magical hovering at your back or total disappearance while you have it sheathed.

I cannot think of any game since Gothic2 which made me want to prepare and set out for a journey to explore the area. You look not only like an explorer, but the game will make you use every piece of it.

Weather/graphics:
- weather effects are present. It startet to snow and some time later, there was a light blanket of snow on the before green pastures and trees.
- after some more time, there was a thick snow blanket on the ground, bushes and trees. Even the buildings and earth and floor planks inside the starting village where white. What an amazing surprise.
- the graphics are kind of an intended graininess. I find it very fitting to the mentioned effects\details

Survival:
- they are not implemented like in a full survival game. They didn't make me to just rush around to find the next bit to eat or drink constantly. 
- temperature-effects will debuff you quickly when you set out unprepared. You need to drink more often when its hot, you will slowly freeze when it is too cold.

So these dangers are always looming in the shadows, but preparation helped me a lot so far and makes you able to live with these dangers on your journeys. You cannot totally neglect them, but the game is not designed only around them as core-mechanic, so you can enjoy the rest of the game.

There are so many details, which in sum make it very enjoyable for me to play this game which i find far more important than combat and spells and graphics. All the games elements add to each other perfectly imo.

Played for over 100 hours, so make of it what you will.

I like hard games. Souls-like and survival. This game isn't hard, it's broken.

The combat is slow and chunky, the hit boxes are a mess and enemies don't play by the same world rules you do (infinite stamina and no fall damage, for example). When you fight an enemy one-on-one, it's painfully easy... but you never fight anything one on one. Then it’s a tumbleweed simulator with you cartwheeling around trying to find a single opening. Some enemies can also hit you multiple times with the same attack and then when you inevitably die, you get teleported somewhere at random in need of a nap and a sandwich.

So the combat is a bust (and to all the morons who smugly said "git gud",  I'd happily push you back under the frothing surface of whatever septic tank you crawled out of - finding exploits is not "gitting gud", it’s cheesing to make up for shoddy design).

The survival elements are un-challenging and token, more like a pop-up to close than something to resolve.

But the straw that broke the camel's back? The mind-boggling game design choices. Failing quest because they were timed and it wasn't clear?  How about losing 20% of a primary stat PERMANENTLY because killing an NPC ally seemed a bit like a Richard-relocation? Better yet, losing the entire starting village, all your gear & money (essentially progress in this game), unique quest items and access to a class trainer, PERMENANTLY, because you didn’t complete a quest you didn’t know about, because you didn’t happen to speak to the right person, at an arbitrary moment following an unconnected quest in a different region? Oh, and of course that quest was timed and expired while you were away. 

No, just no. These developers clearly think their idea is much more special than it actually is. Look at the achievements – the fact that less than 5% of people who own this game, who spent actual money on this title and devote their free time to it, have completed the first quest for their faction. This game has it’s praises sung to the heaven by a vocal minority of grognards, but most people give up on it and walk away.

Save yourself your time, save yourself you money – you deserve better than this steaming hot pile.

Outward has some good moments but they are unfortunately overshadowed by the negatives. 

The game feels really empty. Not barren in an atmospheric sense, just plain empty and unfinished.

Most of my playtime was spent running. Running is a huge part of this game. You run and run and run and run. Running on foot across pretty much empty maps with very little satisfaction. 
The best/worst decision you can make is to stack movement speed gear and buffs. On the bright side you spend less time mindlessly running, but the faster you run, the faster you go through what little content there actually is. 

There are some inexcusable technical annoyances such as permanent mouse smoothing, hardcoded camera sensitivity scaling difference between X/Y axis, mouse sensitivity variable scaling based on framerate, just to name a few.

Fortunately; it’s a Unity game, so with a little persistence you can teach yourself how to decompile Unity games in order to directly edit the game code and manually patch some of these mistakes yourself. 

Unfortunately; it’s a Unity game, so the game really struggles performance wise with the typical optimization issues you can expect from any indie Unity release.

This game would greatly benefit from being bundled with a .NET decompiler and ReShade.

The core principles of this game are very fun. Start as a nobody, get whooped, grow stronger, become a hero. The crafting is fun and the artwork is nice.
But everything I listed is done better in other games. This game has a few major issues that prevent me from recommending it. One major issue, and as far as I've gotten at this point, was the mid game. I've crafted several fancy armor sets, have like twenty spells and high grade weapons. I still die in about 3 hits to anything mid sized or get mobbed by 3 dudes.
80% of your time in this game is going to spent walking around. Either getting to where you want to go, or trying to find the correct path. There's no fast travel, no mounts, no automatic completion of quests, and the map isn't the most useful. There are several distinct regions with different items, armors and most importantly different trainers. It's incredibly frustrating to have to spend twenty minutes just walking my character to the starting area to turn in materials not native to that region and speak to the trainer there(good luck grinding money in one region to use their trainers). Now to walk 20 minutes back.
Speaking of training/skills, that leads me to my second major issue. Magic + skill progression. When you speak to the man blocking your way from leaving the starting village, make sure you have your favorite weapon type equipped. I did not have it equipped and he gave me a random skill. Now, 30 hours into the game with several regions fully explored, I do not have a single sword skill. I've spoken to about 10 people offering training and not one had a sword skill. But beyond that, it's hard to specialize. I have: a 1-handed axe skill, a 2-handed axe skill, a mace skill, two bow skills, a spear skill, two gun skills, and a shield skill. How does no one is this universe use swords?
Now magic, to obtain magic you have to go on a very dangerous quest and sacrifice your health/stamina to even have mana to use. Fast forward so that you can do special runic magic and have bought every spell you can find not locked behind some lengthy/overly expensive barrier. I can now: push people, protect myself against the weather/ certain damage types, and use a flamethrower as long as I'm holding something lit on fire. At what point can I actually just use a magic missile or something simple? Probably after I grind another 40 hours to get enough money to unlock a skill that isn't clear about what it'll let me do.
This game only works if you enjoy looting the same 5 dungeons in a region, love walking for hours to the same two background songs, and don't have very high expectations. Buy it on sale if you like, but your time would be better spent researching other games that'll scratch this itch.

Outward does not like you, it doesn't want you to play it, it actively feels like it wants you to not play the game, but rather "Experience it."

Outward is probably one of the few games where I feel genuine frustration with, now people keep saying "oh it's so much fun being able to run around and experience the world" and yeah, it is fun, but fuck me if it doesn't want me to think it. >"but DARK SOULS?!" There's a clear escalation in threats in Dark Souls and Soulslike games, weak to strong, but in Outward due to its nature, just slaps enemies everywhere. There was a time where a pair of bandits camped outside the city walls, every time I came out, I'd have to try and fight these two who could chunk my health with easy, while I felt like I was doing no damage to them. "Oh you shouldn't have fought them" but WHY ARE THEY RIGHT DOWN THE GODDAMN ROAD?

Play Dragon's Dogma instead, it still makes you feel lost and confused in a big scary world, but you also get to mount a goddamn Chimera and stab it to death.

The negative reviews on this game are honestly astounding in how inaccurate they are (there's even someone talking about levels which don't exist in this game). This is primarily due to a rough start to the game (notice the time played in the negative reviews vs the positive reviews) which is fair but all these people talking about how they feel like they do no damage, their weapon swings carry no weight, and there's no progress are complaining because they haven't experienced the progress yet. As this game can be compared to Dark Souls, it's like reading the reviews of people who never got out of the Undead Parish complaining about the drake on the bridge being impossible to beat.

Ultimately, this game is dependent on experience and accumulated knowledge. Knowing how to make money, where to find skills, crafting recipes, attack animations for the various enemies, how to deal with environmental issues and sickness, etc are all key to this game and sadly, that makes a steep barrier to entry which is, itself a valid critique. Just temper those negative reviews with the understanding that all the gameplay elements they complain about have solutions those reviewing are not aware of.

If you're interested in trying Outward, just understand the game actually has no grinding besides the accumulation of personal skill and knowledge and that the early game without those will be rough. Come up with clever solutions to problems, make use of things like status effects against enemies you lack the damage to properly fight, and do not feel restricted to any particular routes or locations. If you struggle with an area or don't want to address it then, simply don't and go explore somewhere else.

This game is a masterpiece, it's not a souls-like so don't go in expecting fast paced gameplay. Outward is all about preparation, knowing your enemies, managing your resources and learning how to survive! Now let me be clear this game is not perfect, it can feel empty at times and it doesn't have a lot of voice acting and no cutscenes at all. I personally like the combat system but before you understand it, it'll feel outdated and even after you do it's not gonna be the main draw of this game that is meele combat. Review at 50 hours of playtime, i'll probably update this when I eventually finish the game - The first 10 hours were a struggle... but after learning the game's mechanics, this game became pretty fun and reminds me of a cross between fallout 3 (for the open ended exploration element) and dark souls (for the combat element - though of course the combat system in dark souls is a lot smoother).

For a better review, and what personally got me interested in this game, watch Sseth Tzeentach's youtube review on Outward. Another really good review was done by Mortismal Gaming's youtube channel as well.

What's very interesting is that there's a narrative RPG element to the game. When you die, a defeat scenario plays out (think of a 3rd person narrator/game master that role plays what happens if you die/pass out). Often times, the scenario is that you wake up as a captor of some bandit group or rescued by a friendly faction and are under their care. The concept of death in this game is actually a continuation of your personal storyline and makes it much more immersive than a "YOU DIED" death state.

Example: I was venturing out into the Marshland area for the first time and there are some scary dinosaur/raptor enemies wandering around. they often block your path, but you can figure out ways to sneak past them - i accidentally fall off some kind of ledge and into the marsh, which is toxic and quickly decays my health to 0. The scenario that plays out is that I was "rescued" by a bunch of bandits who ended up stripping me of all my gear and leave me for dead in a nearby house.. your player character wakes up a few hours later in that abandoned house - naked .. I end up scavenging my immediate area for supplies and gear while searching the buildings in the area for my backpack and gear. Armed with only a basic sword and rags for clothes, i cautiously approach a larger house and find that everyone there is already dead. Apparently one of the raptor/dinosaur things had already killed the entire camp while i was blacked out from marsh toxins. Hilarious. I find the room in the back with my treasure chest and quickly run like mad to get out of the marshlands as fast as possible.

If you like that 3rd person exploration that's reminiscent of FALLOUT 3 and a combat system that is similar to Dark Souls (just not as well executed) - you'll enjoy this game. I think that it takes elements of each and really makes its own complete game. 

The cons of the game are actually elements that actually make this game a challenge in its own unique way. The tutorial of the game's system and mechanic are actually included as dialog in the first town you start in. Talking to the town blacksmith, for example, explains combat mechanics. Talking to the town fishmonger explains food mechanics. 

What will most likely be something that will be very jarring for new players is map system - you don't get a nice map with a GPS indicator of where you are.. You get a plain geographical map where immersing yourself in the game's environment and finding land marks to estimate where you are on the map like a tourist in a foreign country is how navigation works. That's right- no mini-map or quest markers to guide your direction. It's a bit agonizing at first, but the intention is to get a sense of exploration and adventuring that a lot of games seem to be missing out on with the implementation of "your quest objective is marked on your mini-map" style navigation.

If this sounds interesting and you'd like to watch some YouTube reviews, Sseth Tzeentach's review of this game is hilarious and really got me interested. For a better explanation of the game's mechanics as well as complete descriptions of the learning curve difficulty, watch Mortismal Gaming's review.

So after well over 10 years on Steam and after collecting an embarrassing amount of games i decided to write my first review...

I really like this game it very pleasantly scratches MY itch.

I was at first surprised at the amount of really negative reviews but after a while i felt like most of them originate in very specific expectations not being met.
This title certainly isn't for everyone - and all the following points are MY projections:

This experience is not about mass appeal but rather a very specific vision by the developers - it feels like a game they just really wanted to make.
A minimal amount of research reveals all the points some users have such a big problem with, like the lack of a map, fast travel or even a deliberate saving system.

I was simply blown away when i learned just how small the development team is. Don't get me wrong, at no point does this resemble a triple A title but it still has a very high level of visual beauty, consistency and polish.
I was forcefully reminded of high production values where it seems they spent an insane amount of resources on individual model details and textures but things like menus and inventory management where you spent a considerable amount of time came as an afterthought at best and can be an absolute chore.
Not here. For me at least everything feels very thought out and deliberate.

I like to compare the aesthetic to that of a simple pencil drawing as opposed to to a big oil canvas: a skilled artist can create  something amazing with just a few pencil strokes where as even the most expensive resources will not offset a poor set of abilities...

I feel like a very heavy factor in design decision was the lack of resources. But often i find myself being truly stunned how well those decisions were made and resources were utilized.
Obviously that's very subjective and i can see how others will prefer the focus to be differently distributed...

To bring these rumblings to an end:

I really enjoy this work. I soaked up the atmosphere and found myself wanting to experiment more and more with different skills equipment and story arks.
I'm really thrilled to have  learned that the game is being expanded upon. 
Thanks for again sparking my curiosity!!

I like this game, more than I expected really. But I cant recommend it to everyone since this game requires a specific taste.

Outward tossed out every aspect that I hated in other RPGs. This is what Outward does not have (which is a good thing)
- There are no player levels! 
- There is no difficulty scaling of enemies
- There are no class restrictions
- It does not have a corny hero fantasy story.
- There is nothing that helps you out in the beginning, no guidance or mapmarkers or any form of direction.

What the game doesnt do well..
- Stale presentation of NPCs, gameworld and story.
- Half done voice overs.
- Clunky combat and UI.
- Co op bugs
- non Co op bugs
- Lower graphics than Skyrim
- No fast travel system
- Mediocore music 
- poor character creation options

Most of you would think, this game is bad! And yes, if you are put of by this list dont buy it.

Then why recommend? 
- This is one of the few open world games that can be played in Co-op, which is a huge plus for me at least. 
- The game feels immersive. Camping, drinking, eating and crafting have a meaning in this game. 
- The dungeons and lighting effects are very well done, dungeon crawling is scary, immersive and suprising.
- The weathet and temperature differences are a very nice feature. It makes you prepare before setting out on a journey to the desert or snow.
- There is a wide variety of armor sets, weapon skills, character build options and cosmetic items that can get you hooked for a long time to try them all out.
- The game world has 4 different zones which have a lot of secret places to explore, its really a joy to explore these places for the first time.

There is much to put you off and much to draw you in. Like I said, Outward is an acquired taste.

This is a fantastic game, but definitely isn't for everyone, let me explain.

First off: It have very little voice acting, it does exist but it is mostly just text, which can be tiresome after a while.

Second: There is almost no tutorial, the one that exist will only cover the basic and is even lacking in those regards as well. All the advanced stuff you have to figure out yourself.

Third: The game is hard and unforgiving, oh you got attacked by a hyena and got bit once? And now you have an infection and your bleeding? But you don't have bandages or antiseptic? Welp, guess you better run like crazy towards town so you don't bleed to death, but be careful as every stamina expense takes away some of your maximum stamina until you get some sleep.

Fourth: It is very slow pace, rushing into combat will be a sure way of getting killed, even just rushing out into the wilderness without the proper clothes for different environments or potions to deal with poison and infections will also get you killed.
A lot of the game is preparation and figuring out solutions to problems.

Fifth: No saving, all the choices you do is final, even if you die it doesn't give you a game over and let you retry, no, if you get beaten down, you will respawn somewhere else with a lore explanation of how you survived. This Review is for you, that like me, love challenging and hard games and was willing to overlook a few of the negative comments to give this game a try.

The problem with this game is NOT in its difficulty.
With Outward 2 coming out already, I doubt this review could change anything, but I wanted to warn other players on what they are actually getting into.

The survival system is awesome, it's great to see a game bringing the craft system into a Must Learn situation, and tieing it with the exploration mechanic - so you explore to find items that let you explore even more! That is the cern of adventure, and the feeling is VERY welcoming! Battling climate as much as fighting against a strong enemy is very very satisfying.

The problem for those unaware is: This is not a save-reload-after-failing game like Gothic, or a check-point-to-point system like Dark Souls. In this game, death is canon. Everytime you are defeated you get a random event that moves things around. So if you get a really strong enemy and you are defeated while learning its move set, it could mean, for example, that you are captured by a group of bandits and sent to work on a mine as a slave. This is cool, it's a different take, but it can be very frustrating because now, to have another shot on that enemy, you kinda need to play an extra half an hour of a diferent history to be able to leave the imprisioment.
It's still entertaining, since you are seeing a "quest" that you're not going to see if you weren't defeated - but other situations like "You've been found by a hunter and brought back to your home town" means that you will waste about an hour of gameplay just to walk back to the point where you were defeated, to try again. This is NOT "difficulty", this is TEDIOUS. The game actively makes you WASTE time - both ingame and of your real life. This is not why I'm playing. (It can be worse, seeing some comments said there are quests tied to in-game time).

I'll give you a full example that happened to me: 12h of gameplay in the first area, gathering resources, forgin equipment, training, cleaning up. Got to a new area - started fighting a fire-lizard that was clearly overleveld from myself, but that is okay, dodge-dodge-repeat. During the fight, two bandits come over and start attacking both me and the lizard. Managed to kill both bandits but lost to lizard. Got the "Bandits took your equipment away and stashed it over a house in the north." event. Wake up naked next to a new cool sword (cool, at least got something) - walked north to try and find my 12-hours-investment, have to fight the bandit protecting the stash - WAY stronger than the previous ones - lost. Got the "God saved you from death, you wake up seeing its light" waking up in a random area of the map of that new area I just came in. So I didn't know where I was, didn't know where the bandits took my equipment, and just felt completely ripped off. Again, this is not "difficulty" this is tedious. It means griding those 12h again to get to that same point? Is this fun? Not even FromSoftware is this brutal punishing players.

I decided to delete that character and start a new one - now with the knowledge I had of those 12h. I have to tell you - after another 9h of forcing myself to give this a try, I realized I was not having fun.
I really wanted to like this game, there is a lot about it that makes me want to play, but NOT having fun... the game becomes a chore, and that makes no sense at all.

So if you still think about giving a chance to this, I would say go ahead - now you are aware.
But for the reason stated, I cannot recommend this game to someone.

Maybe co-op could save you from the tedious parts? I don't know, but if you plan on soloing this, now you know.

This game really gets alot of hate, and I can see why many wouldn't like it. My wife and I really enjoy playing this game. There is an extremely steep learning curve for this game. You just have to keep bashing your head against the rocks until something clicks for you. The early game grind gets a bit repetitive, pretty much needing rest after fights with low-tier enemies. But eventually, after using trainers and being patient in combat, you'll be able to explore the first area fully and discover it's far deeper than the map makes it look.

A few pieces of early game advice:
1. Your first purchase should be your home. You can do this easily by selling everything you find in the starting town and maybe hunting a few hyenas. Your second purchase should be a new backpack.
2. Talk to absolutely everyone. I had to pay more because I missed out on high paying quests in the starting town. If they are on your map, talk to them.
3. Blue sand is found on the beach to the south at night. There's also a bunch in a nearby cave. Melee/heavy armor builds will want this material. 
4. Get enslaved by bandits at least once. You learn a lot, and you don't end up losing anything.
5. Get used to walking. It's literally part of the core loop, and an essential part of character building.
6. Start with sword and shield, then build what you want to after you've come to grips with the combat.

This game is not for everyone. It's a slower experience with moments of reflective calm and dreadful terror in equal measure. But once you sink in and become more confident, it's a captivating experience.

Bought it for a whopping TWO DOLLARS on sale and have a buddy to play co-op with, so expect a lot of bias. This is also very much my kind of game, so I will start by saying I don't recommend this game to anyone who NEEDS fast travel, other convenience features, or otherwise does not have time to traverse large maps via steering autorun.

Imagine Dark Souls 2 but with a world that's slightly too open and also heavily limit the character progression. I'd relate the progression amount to a classic Legend of Zelda game but you start with most of the heart containers (i.e. you don't gain much max HP throughout the game). Most of your character's power comes from putting together a tool kit that works together and covers enough situations, with no way to scale your numbers higher than the dangerous enemies like Manticores (and the admittedly bullshit, juiced elite bandits). There is some room for brute force, but even then you have to put some effort and thought into how you approach a situation. Also, all progression is through gear, crafting knowledge (you can make things with wiki knowledge, experimentation, or what you remember from videos/previous save files), and spending money on skills, either passive or active.

If you like outsmarting and/or cheesing things stronger than you, you'll probably enjoy the combat once you understand how the game works. Mainly, you'd best get used to needing supplies for your adventures. Getting through anything but the lowest threat encounters without spending resources (food, potions, ammo, etc.) is quite difficult. Magic is rather indirect, coming in several forms, requiring specific equipment, using consumables, and usually some chance to set yourself up before drawing the enemy into your prepared engagement. Melee combat is honestly flawed, with enemies lacking patterns and self-preservation, forcing the player to learn to force openings or just know when and where you can take hits. Archery is relatively safe, but arrows take carry weight and switching to a melee weapon when pressed will likely require one of your 8 quick action slots.

Exploring in Outward legitimately feels satisfying (if you, as an individual, have time to wander). There's plenty to find, albeit the actual quests are scarce for something that feels like an Open World RPG. My co-op buddy and I had a good time completing a standalone dungeon that we did because of a combination of "Because it's there" and to open up a nice shortcut for travel between regions. It may change once I stop ignoring the main quest lines, but the open world part of the game reminds me of Kenshi, letting me just Do Things because I feel like it, while providing decent reward for doing so.

I'd put Outward at about 7/10. It has some major, persistent flaws, but for the right kind of people, it's a very enjoyable game. It really shines in co-op, but it's been nice solo, too. Just remember that Outward is slow, unforgiving, clunky, and definitely not aimed at the modern Gamer(tm) crowd. The game will force you to play by its rules nearly constantly, but if you're alright with that, there's a lot to enjoy.
